Sessions per node (tracked, not an SLA)

The number to track is active sessions per node per minute. A production node at peak has 205 (430 requests per minute). Off-peak, it has 130 (275 requests per minute). Our node passes the SLA at 165 (325 requests per minute). This is 80% of a production node at peak.

Session = distinct prompt_cache_key. Active per minute = sessions with at least one request starting that minute. In flight = sessions with a request open at that moment (sampled every 10 s; production timing for production rows, ours for ours). Production rows: every logged request of both load balancers, divided by 24 nodes (cross-checked against one node's session-hash share: 1,582 vs 1,559 sessions per 15 min, 213 vs 209 per minute). Live production probe (read-only engine counters, Oct 2 05:24 PDT): b300-18 343 requests/min with 24 running, b300-22 336 requests/min with 42 running, 6.9–8.6 M tokens per GPU per minute, none queued. Engines do not see session keys, so live counts are requests; sessions come from the logs. Peak and off-peak hours from the log volume curve: Sep 30 13:00 PDT is the day's peak (equal to Oct 1's 21:00 PDT peak); the lowest hour seen (Oct 1 16:00 PDT) has 0.47× the peak volume, so the deepest off-peak may be nearer 100 active sessions per minute. The logs undercount production by about 1.1× in requests. Updated Oct 2 06:10; source: /tmp/sessstats/hour_stats.py on node 0008 (fleet logs, 10 hours); s3 hourly volume curve; sessions_ours.py on our runs.

A minute can fail several rules, so a row can add up to more than its failed minutes. Counts come from the per-minute records (runs_v3.json), the same ones that draw the strips and the chart. Our runs on this test never fail on errors. It misses minutes on: errors ×33, TPS ×1 (summed over the loads shown).

The causes, in plain words
  • Generation speed at full load (4.42 M). On the fair test (v3.2), the full node passes 15 of 15 minutes at 3.33 M per GPU and 14 of 15 at 3.72 M. At full load (4.4 M per GPU), generation speed is the limit: in the failing minutes each GPU runs 15 to 20 requests with 0.9 to 1.6 M context tokens, and a generation step takes about 88 ms. Four changes on Oct 2 raised generation speed at full load: prompt chunks sized by their cost (+2.7 tok/s), decode-after-prefill off (+2.7 tok/s), the FA4 kernel for the draft model (+4.65 tok/s) and a faster index-score kernel (+3.6 tok/s). Next: a faster top-k and a faster index score for generation steps. (PROGRESS.md Oct 2 04:40 – Oct 3 00:49)
  • Median first token: passes (rule now under 3 s). Fixed Oct 1 20:41. M3.1 is an image-capable model, so the engine tokenised every conversation, turned the tokens back into text and tokenised it all again; our caches only sped up the first pass. Passing the cached tokens straight through (identical tokens on 300/300 real prompts) plus one cache shared by the 8 tokenizer processes cut the median first token at 2.23 M from 0.85 s to 0.54 s; every minute is now 0.49–0.61 s against the 1 s limit. Per request (median): tokenising 0.045 s, hand-off 0.04 s, waiting 0.003 s, prompt processing 0.22 s, first visible word back to the client 0.10 s. (PROGRESS.md Oct 1 19:20, 19:55, 20:45)
  • Slowest 1% of first tokens: fixed at 2.23 M (no longer an SLA rule). Dropped from the SLA on Oct 1, and fixed anyway: a 300k+ token uncached prompt ran 16k-token pieces back to back for 20+ s while its engine generated nothing. One decode step after each piece (Oct 1 21:24) brought the slowest 1% at 2.23 M to 8.2 s, better than production's 10.4 s on the same requests, with every minute at or under 14.5 s. (PROGRESS.md Oct 1 20:05 and 21:25)
  • Prompts processed again at full load. At 4.42 M we re-process 2.75× as many uncached prompt tokens as production: 84% of the extra comes from conversations whose cached prompt was evicted between turns (the largest share after 2–10 minutes idle). More cache memory (0.76, adopted Oct 1 05:52) cut those evictions. (PROGRESS.md Oct 1 03:45 and 05:55)
  • Errors: one client's tool schemas (Oct 3). On another node's sessions (buckets b02+b03), one session sent 218 tools per request, and 44 of them had "type": {}. Our engine rejected all 60 requests of that session with HTTP 400; production served them. The gateway now deletes only invalid type values (TOOL_SCHEMA_FIX_TYPE): the rerun had 0 errors and 14 of 15 minutes passed (was 1 of 15). (PROGRESS.md Oct 3 00:49 and 03:42)

Written Oct 3 03:43 · 43 newer results since

Full reasoning (reflections of the time)

Oct 1 05:55 · Capacity (mem 0.76) at v3.1 0.75×: 1/15 again, but TTFT 1.01 / 4.84 / 18.3 s (baseline 1.19 / 6.53 / 18.2), slow first tokens −42%, extra re-prefill vs production −11%; decode 55 tok/s (baseline 53). Capacity does what the cache analysis predicted (fewer evicted sessions, lower TTFT median and p90) and stays in the config. What now fails almost every minute is decode below 60 tok/s. Both DP ranks of an engine step in lockstep through every MoE layer, so a 0.75 s prefill chunk on either rank also stalls the other rank's decode; mixing prefill and decode across ranks (speculative_skip_dp_mlp_sync) cannot help for the same reason, and overlap scheduling is already on. Decode speed at load is therefore set by how much prefill time there is.

Oct 1 03:45 · Cache-hit gap anatomy of v3_lp_1x (hit_gap.py, same 6,335 requests): our hit 91.2% vs production 96.6% → we prefill 48.3 M uncached tokens where production prefilled 17.5 M (2.75×). 84% of the extra prefill comes from sessions whose previous request we had just served — their prefix was evicted, mostly after 2–10 min idle (13.3 of 30.8 M tokens). Only 15% is replay warm-up coverage. Our device KV pool holds 1.31 M tokens per DP rank (≈13 long sessions) while 62 GB of GPU memory sits unused at mem 0.68; production runs mem 0.80 with ~250 GB host cache per GPU (ours ~177 GB).

How do I read this page?

  1. TPM per GPU = tokens processed per minute (prompt including cached, plus output) ÷ 8 GPUs: the same formula as production's dashboard. Our loads come from production's request logs, which read about 1.44–1.53× lower than production's engine counters.
  2. A minute is in SLA when the median first token (TTFT p50) is under 3 s, median generation speed (TPS) is above 60 tokens/s and every request succeeds (success rate 100%). A load passes only when all 15 measured minutes are in SLA. The SLA changed on Oct 1 (before: TTFT p50 ≤ 1 s, TTFT p99 ≤ 15 s, errors ≤ 0.1%); every run with per-minute records is re-scored, and run notes written earlier still quote the old rule.
  3. Load we sent = the TPM per GPU that the replayed production requests ask for, not what we served. It rises by adding conversations, never by speeding up time.
  4. Production has two numbers. 4.45 M = production on exactly the requests our full-load replay sends; compare our runs with this. 6.27–6.64 M = production's full load per GPU on its own engine counters (Sep 30 13:29–13:34). The engines count 1.1× the requests and about 1.3× the prompt tokens per request that the request logs record, so about 1.44–1.53× the tokens in total, for reasons not yet established. The 4.20 M in older notes is the whole hub's average per GPU over the same 15 minutes.
  5. Production on the same requests is scored minute by minute with the same rule, from its own request logs. It misses minutes on: errors ×33, TPS ×1 (summed over the loads shown).
  6. The 7.00 M goal's basis is not confirmed. Sep 30 notes tie it to production parity on its engine counters ('north star ≈ production parity', Sep 30 13:40); counted that way it sits at about 4.59–4.86 M on this page's request-log axis (7.00 ÷ 1.44–1.53). The chart draws both readings until the owner confirms one.
  7. Test versions: v3.1 (current, first result Oct 2 12:11) = production traffic recorded Sep 30 13:10–13:25 PDT, minus the requests production itself refused (HTTP 429), with the literal-<image> bug fixed. v3 = the same traffic before those fixes. v2 = lighter Sep 28 traffic. Compare runs only within one version.
  8. SIM = the teammates' synthetic benchmark (StandardKernel): a cross-check, never a ranking.
  9. A single run varies by about ±1 minute from run to run (v2 repeat, Sep 30: 10 vs 11). All times Pacific (PDT).

Measuring

TPM per GPU (M)
million tokens processed per minute (prompt including cached, plus output) divided by the node's 8 GPUs: the same formula as production's dashboard. Our loads come from the request logs, which read about 1.44–1.53× lower than production's engine counters.
Load we sent
the TPM per GPU that the replayed production requests ask for. It is what we sent, not what we served within the SLA.
⅜ / half / ¾ / full load
¾, 0.875×, 0.9375×, full, 1.125×, 1.25×, 1.375× and 1.5× load = 3.33, 3.72, 4.02, 4.39, 5.00, 5.57, 5.95 and 6.70 M on test v3.2; ⅜ load = 1.79 M (run on test v3.1 only); half load = 2.23 M (run on test v3.1 only): that share of one production node's logged traffic. Load is raised by adding conversations, never by speeding up time.
Minute in SLA
a minute where the median first token arrives within 1 s, the slowest 1 in 100 within 15 s, median generation speed is at least 60 tokens/s and errors are at most 0.1%.
Passes (15/15)
all 15 measured minutes are in SLA. 14/15 is a fail.
Closest
the run with the most minutes in SLA on the current test (15/15 at 5.97 M, Oct 4 05:51). It is still a fail.
First token (TTFT), p50 / p99
seconds until the first output token, for the median request and for the slowest 1 in 100.
Generation speed (decode)
output tokens per second for one request while it streams.
Prompt processing (prefill)
reading the prompt before the first token. An uncached ('cold') prompt has to be processed in full; one of 300k tokens takes 15 s or more on our engine.
Cache hit
the share of prompt tokens already held from earlier turns of the same conversation. Production's figure for the same requests is shown in brackets.
Production, same requests
how production served exactly the requests we replay, according to its request logs (4.45 M at full load). It misses minutes on: errors ×33, TPS ×1 (summed over the loads shown).
Production's engine counters
the token counters on production's own engines, 6.27–6.64 M per GPU on Sep 30. They count about 1.44–1.53× the prompt tokens the request logs record; the cause is not established.
Request logs (hub logs)
production's per-request logs, which our replay is built from. They show less load than the engines count.
Goal (7.00 M)
the owner's target per GPU. Whether it counts like the request logs or like production's engine counters is not confirmed; on the request-log axis the second reading is about 4.59–4.86 M.
Test v3.1 / v3 / v2
v3.1 (current) replays production traffic recorded Sep 30 13:10–13:25 PDT, minus the requests production itself refused, with the literal-<image> bug fixed. v3 is the same traffic before those fixes. v2 is lighter Sep 28 traffic. Compare runs only within one version.
SIM (simulation)
the teammates' StandardKernel benchmark on synthetic or recorded agent sessions. It is a cross-check and never ranks changes.

Changes

Adopted settings (formerly 'frontier')
the setup every change is tested on top of: 4 engines × 2 GPUs, 32k prompt chunks, 64 requests per engine and draft block 7, plus load-aware session routing (Oct 1 03:56), more cache memory, 0.68 → 0.76 (Oct 1 05:52), cache-first scheduling, longest prefix first (Oct 1 11:05), tokenise once: shared cache across 8 tokenizer processes + no second pass (Oct 1 20:41), one decode step after each prefill step (removed Oct 2 16:50) (Oct 1 21:24), draft model replays its CUDA graph (Oct 2 00:12), pair the two GPUs' prompt pieces (prefill delayer, 30 passes) (Oct 2 01:00), prompt chunks sized by cost (Oct 2 07:15), FA4 attention kernel for the draft model (Oct 2 18:21), faster index-score kernel for prompt chunks (bitwise equal) (Oct 2 23:25), faster top-k for the indexer (bitwise equal) (Oct 3 04:30), faster sparse attention for generation steps (bitwise equal) (Oct 3 13:34), faster sparse attention for prompt chunks (bitwise equal) (Oct 3 15:31), faster index score for generation steps (bitwise equal) (Oct 3 18:58), host cache 20% larger (ratio 3.6) (Oct 3 23:16), KV memory 0.80 with host ratio 3.13 (Oct 4 04:22), MoE kernel capped at 144 SMs when a cache copy can overlap (bit-exact) (Oct 4 05:51) and scheduler host fixes H2+H3 (exact) (Oct 4 09:08).
Change (formerly 'lever')
one setting or code change, tested on top of the adopted settings at one load.
Verdicts
Adopted = in the adopted settings now. Rejected = tried and dropped; the reason is in the row. Baseline = a reference run with nothing changed. Invalid = the run broke and its result does not count. Finding = an analysis, kernel test or quality test with no SLA run. SIM = a simulation.
KV-cache memory (0.68 → 0.76)
the share of GPU memory kept for processed prompts. More of it means fewer conversations get evicted and processed again.
GPU pair (DP ranks)
each of our 4 engines uses 2 GPUs whose attention halves step together, so a long prompt on one pauses generation on both. Production's layout avoids this.
Load-aware session routing
our gateway keeps each conversation on the same GPU pair so its cache is reused, and sends new conversations to the least-busy pair.
Production's router (Dynamo)
the cache-aware router production uses. On our layout it lost cache hits (65.2%–70.8% vs our gateway's 94.4%), so we route with our own gateway.
Draft block (DSpark)
our speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes 7 tokens and the main model checks them in one step. Production uses a different draft (DFlash2) with block 4.
MiniMax's prompt-attention kernel (MSA)
MiniMax's sparse-attention kernel for prompt processing. In a standalone test (Oct 1 08:02) it was 1.9–2.5× faster than ours with identical output. It does not run inside our engine yet: its toolchain clashes with our engine image (parked Oct 1 09:45).
Where passing collapses (formerly 'knee')
the load between a run with most of its minutes in SLA and one with few. On test v3.1 it lies between 5.95 M (15/15) and 6.70 M (7/15).

Full reasoning (written Oct 1 09:35)

As written then; the numbers line above is authoritative.

Adopted config at 1.79 M per GPU (0.375×): 13/15 minutes; TTFT 0.85 / 2.75 / 6.79 s (production on the same requests 0.34 / 2.95 / 10.4 s); decode 92 tok/s (production 67); 0 errors.

At this load the tail and decode are already better than production; what fails is the median TTFT, by 20–50 ms in 2 minutes. Warm requests (< 1k new tokens) show a TTFT floor that grows with the total prompt length — 0.39 s under 20k tokens, 0.87 s at 60–120k, 1.34 s at 120–250k, 2.0 s above 250k — about 5 µs per cached token. That is not GPU math (the new tokens are few): candidates are chat-template rendering and tokenisation of the whole prompt in Python on every turn (production tokenises in Rust in its Dynamo frontend) and re-loading evicted prefixes from the host cache.

Full reasoning (written Oct 1 07:05)

As written then; the numbers line above is authoritative.

0.5× under protocol v3.1 (2.23 M per GPU): 9/15 minutes, TTFT 0.89 / 3.69 / 14.3 s, decode 77 tok/s (production 65.5), 0 errors.

Median TTFT and decode beat the SLA in every minute but one; the misses are five p99 spikes in minutes that contain 300k+-token cold prompts. Those prompts need ≥ 15 s of prefill on one GPU at ~20k tok/s (production ~10 s for the same ones) and stall their whole engine meanwhile. The 0.5× knee is set by single-request prefill speed, the same bottleneck the 0.75× runs point to.

Full reasoning (written Oct 1 05:55)

As written then; the numbers line above is authoritative.

Capacity (mem 0.76) at v3.1 0.75×: 1/15 again, but TTFT 1.01 / 4.84 / 18.3 s (baseline 1.19 / 6.53 / 18.2), slow first tokens −42%, extra re-prefill vs production −11%; decode 55 tok/s (baseline 53).

Capacity does what the cache analysis predicted (fewer evicted sessions, lower TTFT median and p90) and stays in the config. What now fails almost every minute is decode below 60 tok/s. Both DP ranks of an engine step in lockstep through every MoE layer, so a 0.75 s prefill chunk on either rank also stalls the other rank's decode; mixing prefill and decode across ranks (speculative_skip_dp_mlp_sync) cannot help for the same reason, and overlap scheduling is already on. Decode speed at load is therefore set by how much prefill time there is.

Full reasoning (written Oct 1 05:05)

As written then; the numbers line above is authoritative.

Baseline at v3.1 0.75× (3.34 M per GPU; production 3.37 M on the same requests): 1/15 minutes; TTFT 1.19 / 6.53 / 18.2 s; decode 53 tok/s; 0 errors.

Between 0.5× and 0.75× both SLA axes break together: median TTFT moves just above 1 s and per-stream decode falls from 74 to 53 tok/s. The engines are not queueing (10–15 running per rank, KV 30–78%), so the loss is per-step speed: every scheduler step that carries a prefill chunk (up to 16k tokens per rank, ~0.75 s) also stalls all decoding streams on both DP ranks of that engine. Load grows prefill volume, so more steps are long ones.

Fair prompt sharing

An engine ran out of cache memory while processing a prompt and crashed. Root cause patched; the test is queued again.

Full reasoning (written Oct 1 06:25)

As written then; the numbers line above is authoritative.

Fair chunk share at 0.75× crashed an engine (prefill out of memory); the public MiniMax MSA CuTe kernel does not compile on B300 (NVVM backend failure for sm_103a and for the sm_100f family target).

The crash exposes a stock-scheduler hazard: when no KV is free, add_chunked_req falls back to a full 16k chunk (to avoid leaking the chunked request) and allocation fails hard instead of retracting. Fair share raises resident KV, so it hits the hazard at 0.75×. MSA is not a quick prefill win on this hardware: its kernels target SM100 and the bundled CuTe-DSL 4.6.2 NVVM rejects the generated IR for SM103.

Full reasoning (written Oct 1 04:35)

As written then; the numbers line above is authoritative.

Load-aware pinning at v3 0.5× (2.23 M per GPU): 7/15 minutes pass (baseline routing 2/15); TTFT 0.89 / 4.23 / 18.3 s vs production 0.34 / 2.96 / 10.4; decode 74 tok/s (production 65).

Median and decode are at or above production; the misses are tail spikes. Engine logs show the mechanism: a single 270–530k-token cold prompt is prefilled in 16k chunks for 20–35 s and every other request on that DP rank waits (the other rank of the engine slows too, because both step together in the MoE). Three of the five spike sources were requests production itself rejected with HTTP 429 (its admission sheds big cold prompts under pressure); our replay was serving them. Two failing minutes were only the six media-tag errors, now fixed.

Quality is not the blocker for training-off numerics; capacity is: FP8 doubles KV bytes per token, so on today's heavier traffic the cache misses explode (3.6× more cold 32k+ prefills). Production gets the speed from training-off numerics *with* 4-bit KV — that needs their kernels or MSA, not this switch.

Full reasoning (written Oct 1 02:21)

As written then; the numbers line above is authoritative.

Dynamo with strong affinity at v3 0.5×: 0/15, cache hit 70.8% (was 65.2%; our gateway 94.4%), TTFT p50 6.4 s, 575 cold 32k+ prefills; 0 errors.

The router choice is not the problem; the DP-attention layout is. Each of our workers has two DP ranks with separate radix caches; our gateway pins sessions to (engine, rank), Dynamo pins at most the worker and the engine spreads requests over its ranks, so about half the 'affine' requests land on the wrong cache. Production avoids this by running one attention group per worker (TP2, DP off), which our fork does not support. Follow-up check (code): Dynamo 1.5.0 does pass routed_dp_rank and our fork's DP controller honours it, so the loss is likely in KV events per DP rank (if only rank 0's zmq endpoint is subscribed, the router sees half the cache).

This is the ≥ 2× engine-efficiency gap to production. The connection resets come from the gateway's 1,024 open-file limit (engines have 65,535).

Engineering between runs

  • First-token anatomy at idle, second pass (planned, Oct 1 12:58): a hold window once that run is serving: the idle anatomy pass, then the engine logs are saved (the 12:06 run's timing logs were lost at teardown)
  • Faster sparse attention (generation steps and prompt chunks, bitwise equal) (adopted, Oct 3 15:31): generation steps: one tile per (request, KV head) for all 8 draft tokens, 6.0× faster bit for bit; twin +23.4 tok/s (+35%). Prompt chunks: a device-built work list (no host sync per layer), 1.8× faster bit for bit, 0 mismatches in 36,000 live calls; twin +4.05 tok/s. Both adopted ref twin v3_ab_sattnv2_cl_1x · PROGRESS.md Oct 3 11:34–13:34 · node kernels/sattn/
  • Faster index-score kernel for prompt chunks (adopted, Oct 2 23:25): a warp-specialized rewrite of the indexer's score kernel: bitwise equal, 3.9–5.0× faster on long prompt chunks (58–66% of FP8 peak vs 12.5%); GSM8K 96.74%; full-load twin: generation +3.62 tok/s, 12/15 vs 7/15 minutes ref twin v3_ab_isv2_cl_1x · PROGRESS.md Oct 2 21:34–23:25 · node kernels/idx/
  • Faster index score for generation steps (bitwise equal) (adopted, Oct 3 18:58): bit-exact, 1.85–2.3× faster on its own. First twin (Oct 3 06:33): no clear change while steps took ~90 ms; re-test on the newest stack (steps ~55 ms): generation +7.86 tok/s (CI +6.0..+10.0), 15/15 in both groups ref twins v3_ab_isvv2_cl_1x and v3_ab_isvv2b_cl_1x · PROGRESS.md Oct 3 06:33, 18:58
  • Faster top-k for the indexer (bitwise equal) (adopted, Oct 3 04:30): a threshold-filter top-k with an exact fallback for ties: bit-equal on GPU and on live traffic (38,400 calls, 0 mismatches); 6.8–10.1× on prompt chunks, 3.8–5.5× on generation steps; full-load twin: generation +2.94 tok/s, 12/15 vs 11/15 minutes ref twin v3_ab_tkv2_cl_1x · PROGRESS.md Oct 3 01:42–04:30 · node kernels/idx/topk_v2.py
  • FA4 attention for the draft model (adopted, Oct 2 18:21): production's draft attention backend; at full load generation +4.65 tok/s (95% CI +3.6..+5.9) with the same draft acceptance (3.60). It only pays since the draft replays its CUDA graph (Oct 2 00:12): before that, launch overhead hid the kernel time ref twin v3_ab_dfa4_cl_1x · PROGRESS.md Oct 2 18:21
  • Verify fewer draft tokens per request (DSpark ragged verify) (parked, Oct 2 20:15): the fork's 'compact' mode cannot run on our stack: a boot guard stops it with DP attention and CUDA graphs, our attention path assumes 8 rows per request (wrong outputs), and DP padding keeps the MoE work at 8 rows per request. The verify width is only ~26% of a step, so an engine rewrite waits behind the indexer kernels ref PROGRESS.md Oct 2 20:15 · node serving/ragged/
  • Fused verify kernels for 4-bit KV (planned, Oct 2 00:55): production's in-house verify kernels let it keep 4-bit KV with speculative decoding and training-compatible numerics off; profile our verify step first (index, top-k, sparse attention shares) before writing our own ref PROGRESS.md Oct 2 00:55
  • Attention over both GPUs (our own patch) (planned, Oct 2 00:55): production runs attention split over the two GPUs of a worker (no lockstep); our training-compatible numerics force attention onto one GPU. A max-type index score can be merged across GPUs exactly, so our own patch could lift that guard (estimate +6–15% generation speed at 3.34 M; large effort, GSM8K check needed) ref PROGRESS.md Oct 2 00:55
  • MiniMax's prompt-attention kernel (MSA) (parked, Oct 1 22:55): now loadable in our image (a one-line gate fix compiles it; prebuilt objects link), but prompt attention is only ~11–23% of prompt time, so the expected gain at 3.34 M is +1–4 tok/s; a 15-minute GPU check for identical output comes first ref PROGRESS.md Oct 1 22:45
  • Pair the two GPUs' prompt pieces (prefill delayer) (adopted, Oct 2 01:00): the built-in delayer holds a lone prompt piece up to 30 scheduling passes so both GPUs process prompts in the same step; with the draft-graph fix it lifted 3.34 M from 11/15 to 15/15 (generation 64.1 → 74.5 tok/s, median first token 0.65 → 1.45 s) ref PROGRESS.md Oct 1 22:45
  • Draft model replays its CUDA graph (adopted, Oct 2 00:12): the draft captured CUDA graphs but never replayed them with DP attention on; the gate fix took 3.34 M from 2/15 to 11/15 and generation from 51.5 to 64.1 tok/s (production 64.8) ref serving/minimax-m3.1/patch_draft_local_graph.py · PROGRESS.md Oct 1 22:55
  • Tokenise each prompt once (adopted, Oct 1 20:41): for requests without images the engine passes our cached tokens through instead of decoding them to text and re-tokenising (identical tokens); with the shared cache, median first token at 2.23 M 0.85 → 0.54 s ref serving/minimax-m3.1/patch_mm_pass_ids.py · mm_ids_verify.py · PROGRESS.md Oct 1 19:20
  • Decode step after each prefill (adopted, Oct 1 21:24): after any prompt piece on either GPU the next step generates; at 2.23 M the slowest-1% first token fell to 8.2 s (production 10.4) and every minute passed the old strict rule for the first time; its effect at 3.34 M (generation speed) is queued ref serving/minimax-m3.1/patch_decode_after_prefill.py · PROGRESS.md Oct 1 19:45
  • One tokenisation cache shared by an engine's tokenizer processes (kept, Oct 1 19:54): each conversation's previous turn is reused whichever of the 8 processes gets the next one; 2.23 M: 12/15 with every minute inside the median rule (10 and 11 without it) ref serving/minimax-m3.1/patch_tok_shared.py · tok_shared_verify.py · PROGRESS.md Oct 1 18:55
  • Per-request timing breakdown under load (running, Oct 1 19:10): engine timers (sampled every 30 s) put 0.7–1.0 s of the mean first token outside the GPU scheduler, even at low load; the shared-cache run at 2.23 M (started 19:10) logs per-request stamps that split it into tokenising, hand-off to the GPU scheduler and the return path ref metrics_breakdown.py · patch_timestats_detail.py · reqstats_join.py · PROGRESS.md Oct 1 19:05
  • MiniMax's prompt-attention kernel inside our engine (parked, Oct 1 09:45): identical output and 2.16 ms per call vs our 4.81 ms; the gather and scale steps add 1.5 ms (a fused gather could reach about 1.85×). Its toolchain (CuTe-DSL 4.5) and our engine image (4.6) cannot share one process ref PROGRESS.md Oct 1 09:00 and 09:45
  • Faster prompt kernels of our own (planned): autotune our Triton attention and indexer kernels on recorded prompt shapes, checked bit for bit against the current ones ref progress_data.json queued[0]
  • Dynamo retest with per-GPU-half cache events (running, Oct 4 03:33): Dynamo 1.5.0 DOES route per GPU (DP rank) and our engine honours it - the Oct 1 'not pinned' conclusion was wrong. Why the slowest 1% miss

a huge prompt stalls its engine 20+ s

PROGRESS.md Oct 1 20:05: p99 anatomy on tok8sh_05x (slow_reqs.py: 47 streaming requests > 10 s with per-segment times; engine log): three kinds - (1) huge cold prompts themselves (347k/332k/302k uncached: prefill 20.6-23.2 s); (2) small or warm requests queued 10-21 s (e.g. 1k prompt queue 19.4 s, 9k warm queue 21.2 s); (3) first content 6-21 s after prefill done (20 requests with first content > 5 s after the first stream chunk, only 54-927 tokens generated). Engine 0 DP1 02:46:50-19:47 PDT: a 315k cold prompt runs 16k chunks (~1 s each) back to back; only 'Prefill batch' lines (no decode for its 5 running requests for 20+ s), #queue-req 1 -> 7 because every step's 16k budget goes to the chunk (#new-seq 1). Spec + DP attention never mix prefill and decode, so both ranks' decode stops. Fixes queued: decode-after-prefill moved next (tok8shid_dap_05x), then chunk share 0.875 when requests wait (tok8shid_dap_s875_05x: 2k tokens/step left; share 0.5 was rejected at 3.34 M).

Full reasoning (written Oct 1 09:35)

As written then; the numbers line above is authoritative.

Adopted config at 1.79 M per GPU (0.375×): 13/15 minutes; TTFT 0.85 / 2.75 / 6.79 s (production on the same requests 0.34 / 2.95 / 10.4 s); decode 92 tok/s (production 67); 0 errors.

At this load the tail and decode are already better than production; what fails is the median TTFT, by 20–50 ms in 2 minutes. Warm requests (< 1k new tokens) show a TTFT floor that grows with the total prompt length — 0.39 s under 20k tokens, 0.87 s at 60–120k, 1.34 s at 120–250k, 2.0 s above 250k — about 5 µs per cached token. That is not GPU math (the new tokens are few): candidates are chat-template rendering and tokenisation of the whole prompt in Python on every turn (production tokenises in Rust in its Dynamo frontend) and re-loading evicted prefixes from the host cache.

Full reasoning (written Oct 1 06:25)

As written then; the numbers line above is authoritative.

Fair chunk share at 0.75× crashed an engine (prefill out of memory); the public MiniMax MSA CuTe kernel does not compile on B300 (NVVM backend failure for sm_103a and for the sm_100f family target).

The crash exposes a stock-scheduler hazard: when no KV is free, add_chunked_req falls back to a full 16k chunk (to avoid leaking the chunked request) and allocation fails hard instead of retracting. Fair share raises resident KV, so it hits the hazard at 0.75×. MSA is not a quick prefill win on this hardware: its kernels target SM100 and the bundled CuTe-DSL 4.6.2 NVVM rejects the generated IR for SM103.

Plan at the time (superseded; the current plan is Overview › What runs next): Capacity (mem 0.76) is adopted; the remaining levers now run on top of it: DSpark block 4, 16k chunk, longest-prefix-first, 128 running. Kernel profile of one engine

131k-token prompt takes 6.7 s; attention is half

reflection Oct 1 05:25: Kernel profile of the frontier engine (torch profiler, between levers): a cold 131k-token prefill takes 6.7 s on one DP rank (19.5k tok/s); decode with 32 streams keeps the GPU busy only 67–71% of the time. Prefill time on the busy rank: sparse attention 30% (_q8kv4_sparse_partial + combine), indexer 21% (_q8kv4_index_score + top-k), MoE 20%, dense MXFP8 GEMMs 13%. These Q8KV4 Triton kernels run at roughly 12–14% of tensor-core peak; production replaces exactly them with in-house kernels (kv4_prefill_attn_v3, kv4_prefill_index_v3, kv4_index_tpshard) and splits each prompt over 2 GPUs (attention TP2), so its per-request prefill is ~2–3× ours. The scheduler confirms the coupling: with speculative decoding + DP attention, prefill always runs first and the two ranks cannot mix prefill and decode, so any prefill chunk on either rank pauses decoding on both. At 0.75× each rank prefills ~15% of the time → decode paused ~28% → 74 × 0.72 ≈ 53 tok/s, which is what we measured.

PROGRESS.md Oct 1 05:25: Kernel profile (prof_prefill.sh on v3_lp_075x engines, e3): cold 131,072-token prefill on DP0 6.76 s span, 93% busy: _q8kv4_sparse_partial 1.53 s (24%), _q8kv4_index_score 0.95 s (15%), mega_moe 0.93 s (15%), flashinfer blockscaled dense GEMM 0.80 s (13%), _q8kv4_sparse_combine 0.37 s, _topk_index 0.36 s, _ep8_combine 0.20 s, hicache_transfer 0.11 s; idle DP1 also busy 88% (padded idle batch + waiting in mega_moe 1.99 s). Decode (32 x 2k random prompts, 256 tok): busy 71%/67% (CPU gaps), mega_moe 42% of kernel time, sparse partial 15%, dense GEMM 9%. Scheduler (0922 fork): prefill-first; spec + DP attention forbids mixing prefill/decode across ranks (dp_attn MLP sync) -> any rank's prefill pauses decode on both; prefill delayer and speculative_skip_dp_mlp_sync exist (off); prefill CP exists but not for minimax_m3

reflection Oct 1 03:55: Root cause of the recurring 6 HTTP 500s (and one HTTP 400) on real traffic v3: the engine's multimodal loader treats literal '<image>' / '<video>' in user text as media slots. One v3 session carries 6 literal '<image>' strings plus real images → 'More IMAGE tokens found than data provided' → 500; another has HTML '<video>' tags → 400. Production answers both with 200. M3.1's template only uses its own ']<]image[>[' token and the generic tags are not special tokens, so they are plain text. At ~210 requests per minute one error already breaks the 0.1% error SLA, so this bug alone failed 1–3 of the 15 minutes in every v3 run regardless of speed.

PROGRESS.md Oct 1 03:55: v3 HTTP 500 root cause (catch500.sh on lp_05x engines, 03:33 PDT): minimax_m3_vl.py image regex `<image>|<\|image\|>|<\|image_pad\|>|]<]image[>[` matches literal user text; session ck:cb5bf378223 has 6 literal `<image>` + images -> 'More IMAGE tokens found than corresponding data provided' -> StopIteration -> 500; session ck:abda416ddd2 has 2 HTML `<video>` -> 400 'No data iterator found for token: <video>'. Tokenizer: only `]<]image[>[` (200025) / `]<]video[>[` (200026) are special; template emits only those. patch_mm_literal_tags.py applied to 0922-sglang-hicache + 0922-sglang (backups *.pre-mmtags); effective from chainQ

Dynamo with strong affinity at v3 0.5×: 0/15, cache hit 70.8% (was 65.2%; our gateway 94.4%), TTFT p50 6.4 s, 575 cold 32k+ prefills; 0 errors.

The router choice is not the problem; the DP-attention layout is. Each of our workers has two DP ranks with separate radix caches; our gateway pins sessions to (engine, rank), Dynamo pins at most the worker and the engine spreads requests over its ranks, so about half the 'affine' requests land on the wrong cache. Production avoids this by running one attention group per worker (TP2, DP off), which our fork does not support. Follow-up check (code): Dynamo 1.5.0 does pass routed_dp_rank and our fork's DP controller honours it, so the loss is likely in KV events per DP rank (if only rank 0's zmq endpoint is subscribed, the router sees half the cache).

Plan at the time (superseded; the current plan is Overview › What runs next): Routing stays in our gateway: load-aware pinning at v3 1.0× now (chain38), then sizing, DSpark block 4 and 1.5× (chain39). Dynamo revisited only if dynamo.sglang can pass the DP rank or the fork gains attention TP2. Queued after chain39: verify per-rank KV event endpoints for Dynamo workers and retest (could make the production stack usable here).

Layout4 workers × 2 GPUs per node, one attention group per worker (DP attention off)4 engines × 2 GPUs whose attention halves step together (DP attention on; our engine build requires it)Big: prompt processing on one GPU pauses generation on both (profile Oct 1 05:25)
Prompt-attention kernels~18 in-house kernels, including faster 4-bit-KV prompt attention and a fused verifyvendor Triton kernels at ~12–14% of tensor-core peak; MiniMax's kernel was 1.9–2.5× faster with identical output in a standalone test (Oct 1 08:02) but is parked: its toolchain clashes with our engine image (09:45)Big: prompt processing an estimated 2–3× slower per request (profile Oct 1 05:25)
Prompt templating and tokenisationRust frontend renders and tokenises; workers skip tokenisationPython chat template + 4 tokenizer workers per engine + tokenization prefix cache (adopted Sep 30 13:54)Under test: warm first token 0.87 s vs production 0.31 s at 60–120k-token prompts (Oct 1 09:35); the idle pass (Oct 1 11:15) puts the extra time outside prompt processing; per-request timing logs and 8 tokenizer workers are queued (Oct 1 13:05)
Speculative decodingDFlash2 draft, block 4 (accepts ≈2.8–3.0 tokens per check)DSpark draft, block 7 (accepts 3.66 at 3.34 M); block 4 tested Oct 1 07:54, rejectedNot the gap (Oct 1): our generation is faster at 2.23 M (76 vs 66 tok/s, Oct 1 21:24)
Memory · requests at once · prompt chunkmem 0.80 · 128 per worker · 16kmem 0.76 (adopted Oct 1 05:52) · 64 per engine · 32k (16k tested Oct 1 08:49, rejected)Small so far; 128 per engine failed to boot (Oct 1 12:04, graph capture)
Scheduling orderno --schedule-policy in the argv we read (Sep 27), so the engine defaultcache-first: the request with the longest cached prompt goes first (adopted Oct 1 11:05)Small: still 4/15 at 3.34 M, but fewer failing minutes on every rule (Oct 1 11:10)
Host cache (HiCache)ratio 3, write-through, kernel IO, page_firstsameSame
RoutingDynamo router with strict cache affinity + session pinningour gateway: session pinning with load-aware placement (adopted Oct 1 03:56); production's router (Dynamo) tested Oct 1 01:25 and 02:15 at cache hit 65.2% and 70.8% vs our gateway's 94.4%, rejectedSolved at 2.23 M (hit 95.3% vs production 96.8%, Oct 1 21:24)
Admissioncold prompts capped at 600k uncached tokens per worker; ≈0.1% refused with HTTP 429 (b300-18 worker 0: 43 of 41,156, Sep 30 22:50)none; test v3.1 does not send the requests production refusedSmall
Numericstraining numerics off, with its own 4-bit KV kernelstraining-compatible; production-style numerics (8-bit KV) tested Oct 1 00:25: same quality (GSM8K 96.74% vs 96.21%) but half the cache capacity, so rejectedNeeds their 4-bit KV kernels first
Result on the same requests (derived)per minute: 12/15 at 3.37 M; 12/15 at 3.77 M; 12/15 at 4.07 M; 13/15 at 4.45 M; 11/15 at 5.06 M; 11/15 at 5.64 M; 12/15 at 6.00 M; 8/15 at 6.76 M; 13/15 at 1.79 M (test v3.1); 12/15 at 2.24 M (test v3.1); see its failing rulespasses up to 5.93 M; 15/15 at 3.33 M; 15/15 at 3.72 M; 13/15 at 4.02 M; 15/15 at 4.39 M; 15/15 at 5.00 M; 15/15 at 5.57 M; 15/15 at 5.95 M; 7/15 at 6.70 M
Where two reads disagree
  • max running 128 per worker (serve.yaml, Sep 30); the Sep 27 argv read showed 256
  • draft: DFlash2 block 4 (serve.yaml); Sep 27 notes called it DSpark block 4
  • 429 rate: the serve.yaml note says 0.5–1% under prefill pressure; the worker counter on Sep 30 22:50 shows 0.10% (43 of 41,156)

DFlash2 = production's block-4 draft; ours is DSpark block 7.

On v3.1 requests our generation speed already beats production's at 2.23 M (76 vs 66 tok/s, Oct 1 21:24). The gap is prompt-processing speed, the two-GPU lockstep and per-request time outside GPU math. (This retires the older '75 vs 212 tok/s per stream' note, which current data contradicts.)

How do we launch each setup, and with which tools?

Production engine launch (read-only; serve.yaml read Sep 30, argv and env read Sep 27 23:15)

Two reads disagree: the Sep 27 argv shows --max-running-requests 256 and a DSpark block-4 draft; the newer serve.yaml (Sep 30) shows 128 per worker and DFlash2 block 4. The Sep 30 serve.yaml is newer.

router-policy.yaml

worker_selection:
  prefill: strict-affinity        # the prefill hop owns the prefix cache: overlap-first after two floors, then load
  aggregated: strict-affinity     # the unified (aggregated) pool routes the same way
  decode: default                 # decode hop: Dynamo's load-only default
  instances:
    - name: strict-affinity
      type: incore-strict-affinity    # plugin in vendor/libs/dynamo/lib/router-plugins/incore (needs --features custom-policy)
      parameters:
        min_overlap_blocks: 2         # ignore the ~1-block shared chat-template header
        min_overlap_fraction: 0.5     # affine only when overlap > 0.5 x request blocks

What gave the most, and what we learned

What moved the numbers on real traffic (requests production served Sep 30 13:10–13:25 PDT, replayed on node 0008), what exactly we changed, and what we learned. Gains are ranked by effect; loads are M TPM per GPU sent (2.23 M = half a production node's traffic). Under the Oct 1 SLA the remaining limit is generation speed at 3.34 M.

ChangeWhenEffect
MoE SM cap v2: cap only where copies overlap, +4.4 tok/s at 1.375× (bit-exact)Oct 4 05:51 PDTCapping the persistent MoE kernel at 144 of 148 SMs only in graph steps and copy-overlap steps removes the copy stall without the 4-5% prompt cost of v1.
Device KV +15% at equal host tokens: +4.5 tok/s at 1.375×Oct 4 04:22 PDTKV memory 0.76 -> 0.80 with host ratio 3.6 -> 3.13 keeps host tokens and RAM equal and still adds +4.45 tok/s and first token ×0.91.
Host cache +20% (ratio 3.6): +3.9 tok/s and first token ×0.82 at 1.375×Oct 3 23:16 PDTAt 1.375× a larger host cache keeps more long sessions' history: uncached prompt tokens -18%, generation +3.9 tok/s, first token ×0.82.
Faster sparse attention for generation steps: +23 tok/s (+35%) at full loadOct 3 11:34 (build done) – 13:34 PDT (twin)4.4 M twin: generation 67.2 → 89.9 tok/s (+23.4, CI +21.3..+25.1), first token −7%, 15/15 vs 12/15 minutes; kernel 6.0× faster, bitwise equal.
Re-test a rejected kernel after the bottleneck moves: verify index score +7.9 tok/sOct 3 18:58 PDTSame bit-exact kernel: no clear change at 06:33 (steps ~90 ms), +7.86 tok/s at 18:58 (steps ~55 ms after the sparse-attention kernels).
Faster index-score kernel for prompt chunks: bitwise equal, 4–5× faster, +3.6 tok/s at full loadOct 2 21:34 (bench) – 23:25 PDT (twin)4.40 M twin: generation +3.62 tok/s (+5.8%), first token unchanged, 12/15 vs 7/15 minutes; kernel 3.98× faster over 8 shapes, bit for bit.
Faster top-k for the indexer: same blocks, same order, +2.9 tok/s at full loadOct 3 01:42 (GPU checks) – 04:30 PDT (twin)4.4 M twin: generation +2.94 tok/s (+4.4%), first token +3%, 12/15 vs 11/15 minutes; kernel 6.8–10.1× on prompt chunks, 3.8–5.5× on generation steps.
FA4 attention for the draft model: a gain only after the draft graph fixOct 2 18:21 PDT4.39 M twin: generation +4.65 tok/s (+7.6%), first token unchanged, 12/15 vs 10/15 minutes; draft acceptance unchanged (3.60).
Draft model CUDA-graph replay under DP attentionOct 2 00:12 PDT3.34 M: 2/15 → 11/15 minutes; generation 51.5 → 64.1 tok/s per stream (production 64.8 on the same requests).
Prompt chunks sized by cost (shorter chunks over long prefixes)Oct 2 07:15 PDT4.42 M twin: generation +2.7 tok/s (+4.7%), median first token −8%, first-token p99 18.1 → 13.1 s.
Pairing the two GPUs' prompt steps (prefill delayer)Oct 2 01:00 PDT3.34 M: 11/15 → 15/15 (first pass at this load); generation 64.1 → 74.5 tok/s, median first token 0.65 → 1.45 s.
Load-aware session routing in our gateway (vs sessions pinned by arrival)Patch armed Sep 30 20:25 PDT. Runs ended Oct 1 03:15 PDT (4.42 M) and 03:56 PDT (2.23 M). Adopted 03:56 PDT (page_notes setup_current); chainQ.sh base_env already carried it from 03:29 PDT (commit a042954).Load-aware pinning: TTFT p90 18.5 → 4.2 s, p99 87.6 → 18.3 s at 2.23 M; current-SLA minutes unchanged (12/15).
Tokenise once: one cache shared by the 8 tokenizer processes + ids passthrough (adopted)Shared cache built Oct 1 18:55 PDT, kept with tok8sh_05x (run end 19:54); both adopted with tok8shid_05x (run end 20:41, PROGRESS row 20:45)Median first token at 2.23 M fell from 0.90-0.92 s to 0.54 s; every minute 0.49-0.61 s (production 0.34 s).

What changed. SGLANG_MEGA_MOE_SM_CAP_MODE=copy SGLANG_MEGA_MOE_NUM_SMS=144 (hostfix/patch_moe_smcap_v2.py). (Oct 4 05:51 PDT)

Exact change. Both DP ranks vote through the MLP-sync gather because EP2 hangs if the ranks use different SM counts; buffer layout re-checked with DeepGEMM's host query (needed an int(Array) fix found by the first smoke).

Why. HiCache copy kernels take whole SMs; a persistent 148-CTA MoE kernel then waits for them (verify MoE p50 1000 vs 318 us when overlapped). With 4 SMs left free, copies and MoE run side by side.

What we learned

  • A kernel gate can pass while the engine path still breaks: always run a smoke engine before a twin.
  • Apply a costly optimisation only where it pays (here: graph steps and copy-overlap steps).

Caveats. Measured on the old base (KV 0.76, ratio 3.6); the full-node status run combines it with KV 0.80 + ratio 3.13.

What changed. MEMFRAC 0.80 and --hicache-ratio 3.13 (device 1.85 -> 2.13 M tokens per GPU; host stays 6.67 M tokens). (Oct 4 04:22 PDT)

Exact change. --hicache-size was not used: it sizes each hybrid host pool (KV, index-K, draft) to the same GB, which mismatches their token counts.

Why. More device cache means fewer host load-backs (each load-back forces an eager prompt pass and stalls generation on both GPUs of the engine).

What we learned

  • Device and host cache are separate levers: the device part pays even when host tokens stay equal.
  • Keep RAM fixed by trading the host ratio when device memory grows.

Caveats. GPU memory headroom falls from ~35 GB to ~24 GB per GPU; no OOM in the twin.

What changed. --hicache-ratio 3.0 -> 3.6 (host pool 5.56 M -> 6.67 M tokens per GPU; +55 GB pinned RAM per GPU). (Oct 3 23:16 PDT)

Exact change. config only; research wf_5eb3587c-c3d #2 predicted +3.3 tok/s at 1.375×.

Why. At 1.375× the host cache evicts sessions idle for about 2 minutes; their next turn must re-compute the whole history. A 20% larger host pool keeps them longer, so fewer long prompts run and generation pauses less.

What we learned

  • Eviction ORDER did not matter (LRU is near-optimal in simulation); cache SIZE did.
  • Check RAM: full node at ratio 3.6 uses about 2.6 TB of the 3.0 TB.

Caveats. The 1.0x twin of 10-02 showed no gain from more device KV; the gain grows with load.

What changed. Replace the sparse attention of generation (verify) steps with a kernel that computes the same numbers but runs the 8 draft tokens x 16 query heads of one request and KV head as one 128-row matrix tile. (Oct 3 11:34 (build done) – 13:34 PDT (twin))

Exact change. kernels/sattn/sattn_verify_v2.py via patch_sattn_verify.py; env SGLANG_SATTN_VERIFY_V2=1 SATTN_VERIFY_V2_SPLIT=4.

Why. The old kernel ran every (token, head, block) as its own work item with a full 128-row tile for 16 valid rows, so 87.5% of the matrix work was padding, and it read each K/V block 8 times. The new kernel loads each block once per request and fills the tile with real rows. Sparse attention was about 30% of a generation step; it is now about 5%.

What we learned

  • Re-profile after each kernel win: the next bottleneck moved from the indexer to sparse attention.
  • Count useful work, not just kernel time: a kernel that wastes 87.5% of its tiles is the biggest lever even when it looks 'compute-bound'.

Caveats. Twin halves read a few tok/s higher than the full node; full-node runs at 1.0–1.5× follow.

Exact change. kernels/idx/index_score_verify_v2.py; patch applied since Oct 3 05:30 with the flag off.

What changed. Replace the indexer's score kernel for prompt chunks with a warp-specialized rewrite that computes the same numbers. (Oct 2 21:34 (bench) – 23:25 PDT (twin))

Exact change. kernels/idx/index_score_v2.py (variant ws) via patch_idx_score_prefill.py; env SGLANG_IDX_SCORE_PREFILL_V2=1 SGLANG_IDX_SCORE_V2=ws; the verify path keeps the fork kernel.

Why. The old kernel copied each K tile byte by byte, masked blocks that were fully visible and waited for each matrix multiply, so it ran at 12.5% of FP8 peak. The new kernel loads K tiles with wide aligned copies, overlaps loads, multiplies and the epilogue in separate warps, and masks only the boundary blocks. Prompt steps over long prefixes get shorter, so generation pauses less on both GPUs of an engine.

What we learned

  • Measure a kernel against its hardware floor: a 5× gap to peak is a lever even when the kernel is 'only' 20–30% of the time.
  • Keep the arithmetic identical and change only data movement and scheduling: then a bitwise test replaces a quality run.

Caveats. Tiny prompt chunks (under ~1k tokens) are host-bound and gain nothing. The first call per tile size compiles the kernel (one time per GPU process).

What changed. Replace the indexer's top-16 block selection with a threshold filter: find a lower bound for the 16th score, keep only the few candidates above it, sort them, and fall back to the old exact network when a row has ties. (Oct 3 01:42 (GPU checks) – 04:30 PDT (twin))

Exact change. kernels/idx/topk_v2.py via patch_idx_topk.py; env SGLANG_IDX_TOPK_V2=1 (=check runs the old kernel too and compares on live traffic).

Why. The old kernel merged 64 scores at a time with a two-warp bitonic network, about 19 instructions per score, so it was bound by instruction issue. The new kernel touches each score once and sorts only about 16–21 candidates per row. Rows with exact ties take the old network, so the output order stays identical.

What we learned

  • A gate that tests a worst-case input can block a real gain: check what share of real rows the worst case covers before you reject.
  • Run a shadow comparison on live traffic before a twin: it catches what synthetic inputs miss.

Caveats. First token rose 3% (CI just above 1.0); generation is the binding rule. Rows with 16 or fewer blocks always take the exact fallback (cheap).

What changed. Run the DSpark draft model's attention with the FA4 kernel (production's choice) in place of flashinfer. (Oct 2 18:21 PDT)

Exact change. launch DRAFT_ATTN=fa4 (draft attention backend); all other settings as the adopted stack (v3.2 replay, decode-after-prefill off).

Why. Every generation step runs the draft model once and the target model once. Since the draft replays its CUDA graph, the draft step costs only its kernel time, so a faster attention kernel shortens every step. Before the graph fix, CPU launch time hid the kernel time.

What we learned

  • Test a rejected change again after you remove the bottleneck that hid it.
  • Keep a list of changes that showed no gain, and the bottleneck that was active at that time.

Caveats. The twin used half the sessions on 2 engines per group; full-node runs with FA4 follow (v3_full_cl_fa4_0875x, v3_full_cl_fa4_1x).

What changed. Let the speculative-decoding draft model replay the CUDA graphs it already records at start-up. (Oct 2 00:12 PDT)

Exact change. patch_draft_local_graph.py, env SGLANG_DSPARK_DRAFT_LOCAL_GRAPH=1: a dp-local graph runner skips the dp-global can_run_dp_cuda_graph gate in decode_cuda_graph_runner.can_run_graph (uniform and ragged paths).

Why. The runner already treats the dense DSpark draft as local to each GPU (no cross-GPU communication, graphs keyed by local batch size) but still required a cross-GPU 'can replay' flag the draft never sets, so every decode step ran the draft as ~270 separate kernel launches.

What we learned

  • Check that captured CUDA graphs are actually replayed: capture time in the startup log proves nothing about use.
  • Draft-model mistakes cannot change outputs (the main model verifies every token), so draft-side speed fixes are low-risk; watch acceptance length.
  • A single gate in shared code cost ~20% of generation speed at load; per-step anatomy (timed vs untimed time per step) found it.

Caveats. One run; minutes 9–12 (the heaviest prompt traffic) still miss at 50–55 tok/s.

What changed. Cap each request's prompt chunk by its estimated cost: 16k tokens up to a 44k-token prefix, 10.9k at 88k, 5.9k at 200k, 3.2k at 400k. (Oct 2 07:15 PDT)

Exact change. patch_chunk_cost_cap.py (schedule_policy.py PrefillAdder: add_chunked_req and add_one_req), env SGLANG_CHUNK_COST_PIVOT=44000; cost model chunk × (1 + prefix/44k) fitted from the live kernel profile (indexer ~7 ms per layer per 16k chunk at a 200k prefix vs ~2.7 ms for MoE + GEMMs).

Why. The sparse-attention indexer of a prompt chunk reads the whole prefix, so a 16k chunk over a 200k prefix costs ~4.5× one over a short prefix. The two GPUs of an engine step together (MoE every layer), so one expensive chunk stalls its partner and pauses generation on both. Bounding the cost per step evens the steps and shortens the pauses.

What we learned

  • Profile under real traffic before choosing a lever: the synthetic profile hid that indexer cost grows with prefix length.
  • Balance work per step, not requests: placing sessions by in-flight context (same goal, routing side) made things worse; capping per-step cost in the scheduler worked.

Caveats. One twin at 4.42 M; the pivot (44k) is a first guess and is being tuned (22k twin next).

What changed. Hold a lone prompt piece for up to 30 scheduling passes so both GPUs of an engine process prompts in the same step. (Oct 2 01:00 PDT)

Exact change. server args --enable-prefill-delayer --prefill-delayer-max-delay-passes 30 (built into the engine; safe with SGLANG_DECODE_AFTER_PREFILL=1 because both use the all-gathered flags).

Why. With speculative decoding and DP attention a prompt step on either GPU pauses generation on both, and 94–96% of prompt steps ran on one GPU alone. Pairing them halves the number of generation pauses for the same prompt work.

What we learned

  • When two ranks step together, pair their expensive steps; the waiting costs first-token time, which had headroom under the 3 s rule.
  • Measure single-rank vs paired steps from the engine logs before tuning: the 94–96% figure predicted the gain.
  • Stacking matters: the delayer helps most once each generation step is cheap (draft graph fixed first).

Caveats. One run; median first token rose to 1.1–1.7 s, so less headroom remains for heavier loads.

Simulation agentic-quick c64 (cross-check only, never used to rank)827 out tok/s, TTFT p50 3.31 s, per-request speed p50 13.4 tok/s2,765 out tok/s, TTFT p50 0.28 s, speed p50 72 tok/sPROGRESS 22:05 PDT Sep 30 (gap_bench: chain36 engines with the same settings, gateway with poolrank + arrival pinning) and 04:50 PDT Oct 1 (v3_lp_05x engines, load-aware pinning)

What changed. The gateway still pins each conversation to one engine DP rank (slot), so its cached prompt is reused. A new conversation now goes to the slot with the fewest requests in flight. On its next request, a conversation moves if its slot has more than 16 requests in flight above the least-busy slot. (Patch armed Sep 30 20:25 PDT. Runs ended Oct 1 03:15 PDT (4.42 M) and 03:56 PDT (2.23 M). Adopted 03:56 PDT (page_notes setup_current); chainQ.sh base_env already carried it from 03:29 PDT (commit a042954).)

Exact change. Gateway shim.py patched by serving/minimax-m3.1/patch_shim_loadpin.py, which builds on patch_shim_slots.py, patch_shim_session.py and patch_shim_balance.py (in-flight counters). ROUTE_PIN_BY_INFLIGHT=1: new session → slot with the fewest in-flight requests; ties go by estimated tokens arrived in 120 s, then arrivals in 30 s. ROUTE_REPIN_SLACK=16: re-pin when slot in-flight > least-loaded + 16. Unchanged: ROUTE_SESSION_KEY=prompt_cache_key,cache_salt and ROUTE_BALANCE_SLACK=1 (chainQ.sh base_env); ROUTE_DP_SIZE=2 (launch_tp2x4_old.sh; 8 slots = 4 engines × 2 DP ranks). run_gateway.sh line 35 forwards both new vars and chainQ.sh base_env sets them. /health route.repin counts moves.

Why. Arrival pinning placed each new session by tokens arrived in the last 120 s and never moved it, ignoring work in flight: at 2.23 M one engine queued 43-66 requests while three ran 2-13. Placing by in-flight count, and moving a session whose slot runs more than 16 above the least-loaded, spreads load and keeps hit (94.4% → 94.6%).

What we learned

  • Pin sessions for cache locality but place new ones by live in-flight count, and re-pin when a slot runs far above the least-loaded (22 moves at 4.42 M).
  • A router needs stickiness and load-awareness together: arrival pinning piled load on one engine; spreading without rank stickiness lost cache (Sep 28 hash+spill 86.6% → 81.0%; Dynamo 65-71%).
  • Check per-slot in-flight counters every run: twice about half the DP ranks sat idle (hash-digit bug, Sep 27 23:53; arrival pinning in v2 1.0x, Sep 30 20:25).
  • A TTFT-median-only SLA hides routing faults: arrival pinning kept every minute's p50 under 3 s at 2.23 M while p99 reached 87.6 s and one engine queued 43-66.

Caveats. One run per arm, on test v3. Production-429 requests were still replayed (3 stall sources were 357-420k-token prompts) and media-tag 500s were present. The gateway open-file limit was raised between the two runs, but neither run had connection resets. Under the current SLA both arms score 12/15 at 2.23 M; the measured gain is in the tail and under the old strict rule. No arrival-pinned run exists at 3.34 or 4.42 M on v3/v3.1; the higher-load pile-up evidence is the v2 1.0x diagnostic (tc0kv8_1x, 2.94 M/GPU). Placement counts requests, not prompt tokens: a 300k-token cold prompt counts as one in-flight request. By design a re-pinned session pays one cold prefill on its new slot (patch docstring; not measured). runs_meta.json says traffic piled onto 2 of 4 engines; that matches the v2 1.0x diagnostic. The v3 2.23 M diagnostic shows one hot engine (e0).

What changed. Two changes, kept together. First, each engine's 8 tokenizer processes publish every tokenised prompt to a shared in-memory folder, so a conversation's next turn reuses the previous turn's tokens no matter which process gets it. Second, requests without images, video or audio pass those token ids on to the scheduler, instead of text that is tokenised again. (Shared cache built Oct 1 18:55 PDT, kept with tok8sh_05x (run end 19:54); both adopted with tok8shid_05x (run end 20:41, PROGRESS row 20:45))

Exact change. Env on top of load-aware pinning + MEMFRAC=0.76 + --schedule-policy lpm: TOKW=8 (--tokenizer-worker-num 8), SGLANG_TOKENIZE_PREFIX_CACHE=1 (on since Sep 30), SGLANG_TOKENIZE_PREFIX_CACHE_SHARED_DIR=/dev/shm/m31tokpc (defaults _SHARED_BOUNDARIES=64, _SHARED_GEN_S=600, _SHARED_KEEP=3), SGLANG_MM_PASS_IDS_WITHOUT_MEDIA=1. Patches on /data01/minimax31/src/0922-sglang-hicache/python: patch_tok_shared.py -> sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/tok_prefix_cache.py (backup .pre-tokshared); patch_mm_pass_ids.py -> serving_chat.py (backup .pre-mmpassids). Both are off when the env is unset. Engines run --ipc private with a 64 GB /dev/shm each, so there is one cache per engine. Run: v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8shid_05x.

Why. Connections reach the tokenizer processes at random, so a per-process cache found a session's previous turn only by chance; mostly it matched just the shared system prompt, saving 32% of what one cache would. Publishing each tokenised prompt to /dev/shm as int32 ids plus boundary index files recovers 99.5%. Passing the ids through removes the second, uncached encode.

What we learned

  • Behind a random load balancer, a per-process cache sees a session's previous turn only by chance. Share the cache across processes or route by session before judging it.
  • Score a prefix cache by characters saved against one ideal cache, not by hit rate. Ours 'hit' on 98% of calls yet saved only 32%.
  • On every lookup, take the longest prefix found in the local or the shared store. Checking the shared store only after a total local miss gave just 2 shared hits.
  • Keep cross-process cache housekeeping off the hot path: atomic rename on write, time-bucketed directories, deletion by an external rm -rf, no scans of cache files inside the process.

Caveats. Under the current SLA it changes no pass count at 2.23 M (15/15 before and after). At 3.34 M every miss is decode (median TTFT already 0.98 s, v3_lp_cap_lpm_075x). Tokenise-once at 3.34 M and at 1.79 M: not measured (tok8shid_0375x was dropped at 20:55; the 3.34 M baseline is queued). The passthrough ran only on top of the shared cache (0.85 -> 0.54 s), and the shared cache only without it; the passthrough alone was never run. Warm 200k+ prompts still spend 3-7 s tokenising in about a quarter of cases (336 requests: p50 0.148, p75 3.27, p90 4.25 s), even though offline replays hit the cache. CPU contention is suspected, not proven. One run per configuration, and identical runs differ by about one minute (PROGRESS 19:10). /dev/shm memory use: not measured.

What changed. After any step in which either GPU of an engine processed a prompt, the next step only generates tokens; prompt processing resumes the step after. (Patch Oct 1 19:45 PDT; run finished and adopted Oct 1 21:24 PDT (test v3.1, 2.23 M).)

Exact change. patch_decode_after_prefill.py on the 0922-sglang-hicache tree (sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py, backup *.pre-dap): if SGLANG_DECODE_AFTER_PREFILL=1 and last_batch.is_extend_in_batch (all-gathered, identical on both DP ranks), the step skips get_new_batch_prefill and only decodes. Env set via EXTRA_ENV in chainQ lever v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8shid_dap_05x (trace b00, frac 1.0) on MEMFRAC=0.76, --schedule-policy lpm, --enable-request-time-stats-logging, TOKW=8, SGLANG_TOKENIZE_PREFIX_CACHE_SHARED_DIR=/dev/shm/m31tokpc, SGLANG_MM_PASS_IDS_WITHOUT_MEDIA=1.

Why. Prefill always went first and, under spec decoding + DP attention, never shares a step with decode. A 315k-token cold prompt therefore ran 16k-token chunks back to back for 20+ s while running requests on both GPUs waited, including first visible text queued behind an invisible think marker. One forced decode step per prefill step bounds that starvation.

What we learned

  • Bound starvation instead of slicing work: one decode step per prefill step fixed the 2.23 M tail; fair share and CHUNK=16384 had worsened p99 at 3.34 M.
  • Decide per-step policy from state every DP rank already shares (all-gathered is_extend_in_batch): ranks cannot diverge and no extra collective is needed.
  • A tail fix can be invisible to a median SLA: 15/15 → 15/15 under the current rule; its value now rests on decode at 3.34 M.
  • On M3.1 (adaptive thinking) the first generated token is usually an invisible think marker; track first visible content separately (lag p99 6.0 s on tok8sh_05x).

Caveats. One run; identical runs differ by about one minute (PROGRESS 19:10 PDT 10-01). Decode dipped at 2.23 M (lower in 10 of 15 minutes, mean −1.8 tok/s, worst minute 68.8 → 63.8); at 3.34 M minutes sit near 58, so the sign matters. Not measured there. Our profile note (m31-engine-profile.md) expects decode interleaving not to raise per-request decode rate (same prefill work). Cold giants now get at most every other step (chunk and decode steps alternate); their own TTFT under the change is not reported. First-content lag was not re-measured after the change.

What changed. The engine admits waiting requests longest-cached-prefix first (SGLang policy 'lpm'); the fork's default order is not recorded in our notes. (Run finished Oct 1 11:05 PDT and adopted (PROGRESS row 11:10 PDT).)

Exact change. SGLang flag --schedule-policy lpm appended to XARGS (lever_queue.txt line "XARGS=$HCX --schedule-policy lpm"), on MEMFRAC=0.76 and load-aware session pinning (ROUTE_PIN_BY_INFLIGHT=1, ROUTE_REPIN_SLACK=16). Run v3_lp_cap_lpm_075x (b00 + half of b01's sessions = 3.34 M, test v3.1).

Why. Hypothesis, not measured: at ~95% token cache hit, warm follow-up turns need few new tokens; admitting longest-cached-prefix first lets more of them share a prefill step while uncached prompts wait, so fewer decode pauses under the lockstep. It cannot pre-empt a giant already chunking: the chunked request is always admitted first.

What we learned

  • With ~95% of prompt tokens cached, admitting by cached prefix cut the 3.34 M tail (p99 18.3 → 13.4 s) and lifted decode; small costs at lower load.
  • Score each lever per failing rule: 1/15 → 1/15 on the old rule hid gains on all three rules (median, p99, decode).
  • Scheduling gains appeared only under load: none at 1.79 M, tail-only at 2.23 M, tail and decode at 3.34 M; test levers at the load that fails.

Caveats. Single runs; identical runs differ by about one minute (PROGRESS 19:10 PDT 10-01). Small costs at lower load: at 2.23 M the median rose 0.88 → 0.94 s (old-rule median misses 3 → 6, before the tokenisation fix); at 1.79 M decode 92.0 → 88.7. Both still pass the current SLA. Still 11 of 15 minutes at or below 60 tok/s at 3.34 M; the worst minute did not improve (46.0 → 45.6). Production's argv (read Sep 27) has no --schedule-policy, so it runs its engine default, which we have not recorded; parity unknown.

What changed. Gave the GPU KV cache a bigger share of each GPU's memory (static fraction 0.68 → 0.76). The host-RAM cache tier (HiCache, sized at 3× the GPU cache) grew with it. (Gap analysis Oct 1 03:45 PDT. The 0.76 run ended 05:52 PDT (page_notes adopted_at); the queue was rebuilt on top of it at 06:25 PDT (lever_queue.txt note).)

Exact change. MEMFRAC=0.76 → launch.sh --mem-fraction-static 0.76 (line v3_lp_cap_075x in lever_queue.txt, commit a042954). Every lever queued from 06:25 PDT on adds it; v3_lp_f2_075x and the v3_lp_05x_v31 calibration were queued earlier and ran at 0.68. HiCache unchanged: --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 3.0 --hicache-write-policy write_through --hicache-io-backend kernel --hicache-mem-layout page_first, on tree 0922-sglang-hicache with patch_hicache_nvfp4.py. That patch removes the 'MiniMax NVFP4 does not yet support HiCache scale transfer' guard and takes the vendor's draft-pool write-back; correctness check PASS Sep 28 18:36 PDT. Diagnosis tool: serving/minimax-m3.1/hit_gap.py <replay out .jsonl>.

Why. At 4.42 M we prefilled 2.75x production's uncached tokens; 84% of the extra was on already-served sessions, about half after 2-10 min idle, while 61.9 GB per GPU sat unused. mem 0.76 grew the device KV pool 41% and, via HiCache ratio 3.0, the host tier; at 3.34 M idle-session deficits shrank (2-10 min 1.39→1.06 M, >10 min 1.59→0.73 M).

What we learned

  • Classify cache misses by session history and idle gap before tuning: 84% of excess prefill was on already-served sessions, about half after 2-10 min idle, which pointed at capacity.
  • mem 0.72 and HiCache ratio 4 showed no gain at v2 0.5x (KV use ~10%); mem 0.76 cut >10 s first tokens 42% at 3.34 M: test capacity under load.
  • A host KV tier does not guarantee retention: with HiCache ratio 3, sessions idle 2-10 min still cost 13.29 M extra uncached tokens at 4.42 M.
  • Cache gains move tails, not decode-bound minutes: mem 0.76 left 3.34 M at 2/15 under the current SLA because decode stays at or below 60 tok/s in 13 minutes.

Caveats. One run per setting. Identical runs differ by about one minute (PROGRESS 19:10 PDT Oct 1), so 9 → 10/15 at 2.23 M is within noise; the main evidence is the 3.34 M tail and the hit-gap shifts. The gap anatomy came from 4.42 M on test v3; 4.42 M was not re-run at 0.76. Not all of the 84% is eviction. hit_gap's 'seen' class also covers prefixes sent to another slot or never cached. The <30 s bucket is structural: our answers differ from production's, so the next turn's new tail is uncached (memory m31-protocol-v31.md). HiCache was never isolated on v3/v3.1: on/off ran on the v1 staircase (Sep 28) and ratio 4 on v2 0.5x. About 1 TB host RAM was still free at 0.76; a larger host tier was not tested. A Sep 28 closed-loop HiCache result (31.50 M node at 99.8% hit) was invalid: the host cache still held prompts from the preceding staircase (PROGRESS 19:43 PDT Sep 28). Hit is still 95.0% vs production 97.0% at 3.34 M.

Findings

Measurements that changed what we work on.

Attention split across both GPUs (TP2): faster first token, slower generation Finding4.42 M twin: first token −47% (0.66 s vs 1.53 s), generation −13% (48.4 vs 55.7 tok/s).
MeasureBeforeAfterSource
median first token (paired ratio)1.53 s (control)0.66 s; ×0.531 (CI 0.505..0.554)twin v3_ab_tp2attn_1x, Oct 2 09:56

What changed. Run each engine with attention split across its 2 GPUs (TP2, no DP attention), as production does. (Oct 2 08:35 (smoke) and 09:56 PDT (twin))

Exact change. SGLANG_M3_TRAINING_ALLOW_ATTN_TP=1 (patch_training_attn_tp.py) + patch_dspark_tp_ntnp.py; launch DP_ATTN=0 DP_SIZE=1 FORCE_TOPOLOGY=1; gateway ROUTE_DP_SIZE=1.

Why. Both GPUs work on every prompt chunk, so prompt work is about 2× faster and the GPUs do not wait for each other. Each generation step needs an all-reduce of the hidden states in every layer, so generation steps cost more.

What we learned

  • A layout change can move the two SLA rules in opposite directions: check which rule binds before you adopt it.
  • Production pairs TP2 with a fused all-reduce; test the pair, not the layout alone.

Caveats. Group B had no prefill delayer (DP-only feature).

What changed. Replay each follow-up turn with our engine's earlier answers in place of production's (cumulative along the session); warm-up turns with a measured successor generate. (Oct 2 12:15 PDT)

Exact change. replay_v2_cl.py --closed-loop (protocol v3.2); chainQ.sh REPLAY_FILE_A/B and REPLAY_EXTRA_A/B per lever.

Why. Production's cache holds the answers it generated, and a real deployment of our engine would hold ours. Replaying production's answers made us process them again. With v3.2 our cache reuses our own answers, except where the client sends the answer back without its reasoning (then the text differs, for production too).

What we learned

  • Check that the test does not charge the system for work a real deployment would not do.
  • A fairer test moved the numbers a little, not the conclusion: generation speed at full load is the limit.

Caveats. 31% of measured requests have no replayed earlier turn and keep production's history.

MeasureBeforeAfterSource
GPU rank time at 4.42 M (engine timers, measured window)—generating 58%, prompt work 37%, idle 1%metrics snapshots, Oct 2 09:09-09:22 UTC
uncached prompt tokens, same requestsproduction 15.6 Mours 30.1 Mrun v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8shid_dap_dg_pd30_1x
uncached prompt per twin group at KV memory 0.76 / 0.8012.20 M and 11.98 M (0.76)12.18 M (0.80)twins dap3_1x, cap80_1x

What changed. Analysis only: per-request cache hits compared with production on exact parent→child turns, engine timers, production's own engine metrics (read-only). (Oct 2 04:40–04:45 PDT)

Exact change. Excess 15.4 M = 31% sessions whose history predates our warm-up, 26% production reusing the answer it generated itself (its cache holds that answer; ours holds a different one), 43% real loss on ~110 follow-ups of 128k+ sessions. Production: 2.10 M GPU + 6.31 M host tokens per GPU, cumulative uncached ~3.8%, zero cache drops.

Why. Prompt work pauses generation on both GPUs of an engine, so every extra uncached token costs generation speed at full load. The misses come from replay effects (answer reuse, warm-up boundary) and from how the host cache drops entries, not from total cache size.

What we learned

  • Compare cache hits on exact parent→child turns: same-session ordering mixes parallel sub-agents and overstates misses.
  • 97% of 'partial' hits only lose the last page (page size 128); look at the token distribution before blaming the cache.
  • Test capacity before buying it: +15% GPU/host cache moved nothing, so the next lever is the cache mechanism (write-back), not memory.

Caveats. The answer-reuse share is a property of replaying production's prompts against our different answers; a real deployment would reuse its own answers.

What changed. The owner set a new rule: median first token under 3 s, decode above 60 tok/s, 100% success, no p99 rule. Every stored per-minute record, ours and production's, is re-scored when the page renders instead of being re-run. The GPU queue was re-planned around decode speed at 3.34 M. (Oct 1; logged 20:55 PDT (PROGRESS: rule seen on the dashboard 20:50; memory m31-sla-v2: notice 20:11, owner comment 20:33))

Exact change. page_notes.json 'sla' = {ttft_p50: 3.0, ttft_p99: null, decode: 60, errors_pct: 0, minutes: 15}; the old rule is kept under 'old' (1.0 s / 15 s / 60 / 0.1%). progress_page.py rescore() (line 236) re-scores runs_v3.json minutes[] and prod_minutes[] on every render. A minute fails if ttft_p50 >= 3.0 or missing, decode_p50 <= 60 or missing, or it has any error. extract_runs.py still encodes the old rule (docstring, line 35), so the 'passed' it stores is old-rule. page_notes.json run-number placeholders are filled by fill() from the re-scored records. progress_page.py exits 1 and writes nothing on any ERROR, including a complete run with no runs_meta.json entry (partial records only warn). update_progress.sh renders the page, runs dom_test.js and check_layout.sh (390-1440 px), and skips the commit if the render or the tab-script test fails. A layout failure still commits.

Why. The 3 s line is 5-6x the tokenise-once run's per-minute medians at 2.23 M (0.49-0.61 s) and p99 is gone, so first-token time no longer binds. Decode must still exceed 60; the best 3.34 M run decodes 45.6-63.7 per minute. Code reading (05:25): any prefill on either GPU of an engine pauses decode on both; untested as the cause.

What we learned

  • Store per-minute quantiles and apply thresholds at render: the Oct 1 rule change re-scored all 28 stored run records without a GPU minute.
  • When the rule moves, move the test load: every v3.1 run now passes 15/15 at 2.23 M (tok1 went 1/15 → 15/15), so only 3.34 M ranks levers.
  • Re-score the reference too: under 'success 100%' production fails 3 minutes on its own 504s at 2.23-3.34 M, and its per-minute decode at 3.34 M is only 60.1-68.8.
  • Fill run numbers from the records at render (placeholders filled from the run records), never type them; extract_runs.py's stored 'passed' is still old-rule, so read verdicts via rescore().

Caveats. Run notes written before 20:55 still quote the old rule (page_notes.json layout_notice). Our 15/15 against production's 12/15 at 2.23 M comes from production's own 504s, not from more capacity. 3.34 M has no identical repeat, so its pass-count noise is not measured; 10 of the best run's 15 minutes decode within 4.6 tok/s of 60. Re-scoring worked only because the new rule uses quantiles already stored (TTFT p50, decode p50, errors). Missing data scores differently: extract_runs.py passes a minute with no decode samples, rescore() fails it. No stored minute lacks samples today. Planned hardening is not built: fail-closed scoring at extraction, a per-minute uncached ratio, and TPM counted only for tokens served inside the window (page_notes.json engineering). The basis of the 7 M/GPU goal is unconfirmed (page_notes.json goal).

GPU activity while DP0 prefills one 131,072-token cold prompt (6.76 s span; DP1 has no requests of its own)DP0: 93% busy prefillingDP1: 88% busy anyway (padded idle batch + 1.99 s waiting in mega_moe)PROGRESS 05:25 PDT (10-01); prof_prefill.sh phase 1 (one request) on v3_lp_075x engine e3

What changed. Nothing changed; we profiled one engine during a cold prefill and read the fork's scheduler to explain why decode falls as load rises. (Suspected Sep 27 20:10 PDT; confirmed by kernel profile + scheduler read Oct 1 05:25 PDT; decode became the only failing rule at 3.34 M with the SLA change (Oct 1 20:55 PDT).)

Exact change. Layout: launch_tp2x4_old.sh TP_SIZE=2 EP_SIZE=2 DP_SIZE=2 DP_ATTN=1, TRAINING_COMPAT=1; launch.sh refuses attention TP > 1 on this fork ('training-compatible arithmetic requires attention TP1'), so DP attention is required. Tools: prof_prefill.sh (SGLang /start_profile), prof_top.py. Fork knobs present but off: --enable-prefill-delayer (queued at 3.34 M as v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8shid_pd_075x), speculative_skip_dp_mlp_sync. SGLANG_DECODE_AFTER_PREFILL=1 is adopted but measured at 2.23 M only.

Why. Training-compatible numerics force attention TP1, so each engine runs attention data-parallel on its two GPUs with a shared MoE step. With speculative decoding the DP MLP sync forbids mixing prefill and decode across ranks, and prefill goes first, so any prefill chunk on either rank halts decode on both. Paused fraction ≈ 1−(1−p)², p = one rank's prefill share.

What we learned

  • Coupled ranks turn prompt load into decode loss: ~50% more prompt work from 2.23 to 3.34 M cut our decode 76.5 → 53.4 while production stayed ~65.
  • Cheap levers only bound or pair the pauses (decode-after-prefill, --enable-prefill-delayer); the structural fix, attention TP2 like production, is blocked by training-compatible numerics.
  • Profile the idle rank too: with no requests of its own, DP1 was 88% busy on a padded batch and mega_moe waits; utilisation hides lockstep waste.
  • Smaller lockstep groups paid before: four dp2 engines decoded 71 tok/s per stream vs 25 for one dp8 engine (Sep 27 21:49 PDT, M3-era v1 trace, settings differed).

Caveats. Production also runs ~18 in-house kernels, so its flat ~65 tok/s is not the layout alone. The 1−(1−p)² paused fraction is the explanation in memory m31-engine-profile.md, not fitted to measurements; that note quotes 74 tok/s (v3_lp_05x, test v3) for 2.23 M. Our own profile note expects decode interleaving not to raise per-request decode rate (same prefill work). 2.23 and 3.34 M points are test v3.1; 4.42 M is test v3, which still replayed giants production had refused with 429 and had the media-tag HTTP 500s. No remedy measured at 3.34 M yet: decode-after-prefill and --enable-prefill-delayer are queued (PROGRESS 20:55, 21:25; node_state.txt); speculative_skip_dp_mlp_sync untested. Non-training numerics with our 4-bit KV fail to boot (need MSA and no spec decoding; PROGRESS 21:30 PDT 10-01); with 8-bit KV they boot but cache hit fell to 83.5% (v3_tc0kv8_05x).

Root cause: the multimodal model type made the engine tokenise every prompt twice FindingM3.1's image-capable model type forced a decode to text plus a full re-encode: 0.131 s median, 0.695 s p90 per request.
MeasureBeforeAfterSource
