Early signal: py-spy on the frontend, Sep 27 static 80k-prompt frameprompt tokenised twice per request on one thread, ~2 req/s capworked around with 8 tokenizer workers (c64 7.02 -> 12.34 M TPM whole node, TTFT 27 -> 2.9 s). The double pass stayed until Oct 1PROGRESS Sep 27 rows 20:09 and 21:40 UTC (13:09 / 14:40 PDT)

What changed. Nothing changed with this finding alone, but it explains why the Oct 1 tokenisation levers moved the median little or made it worse. The chat handler tokenised the prompt (through our cache). Because the model is registered as image-capable, it then turned the ids back into text, and the tokenizer manager tokenised the whole conversation again with no cache. The fix (pass the ids through) is in the tokenise-once entry. (Oct 1 19:20 PDT. The double tokenising first showed in a py-spy on Sep 27 13:09 PDT (row stamped 20:09 UTC))

Exact change. In sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/serving_chat.py (hicache tree /data01/minimax31/src/0922-sglang-hicache/python), _apply_jinja_template renders and encodes through our tok_prefix_cache (added Sep 30). Stock code then, because is_multimodal is true (model_type minimax_m3_vl), runs `prompt = tokenizer.decode(prompt_ids)`; _convert_to_internal_request sends {'text': prompt}, and tokenizer_manager re-encodes with self.tokenizer([text]). Checked with mm_ids_verify.py --trace <v3 b00> --n 300 (engine image, CPU). Fix: patch_mm_pass_ids.py, env SGLANG_MM_PASS_IDS_WITHOUT_MEDIA=1.

Why. Because model_type is minimax_m3_vl, serving_chat decodes the prompt ids back to text on every request, media or not, and the tokenizer manager encodes the whole conversation again, uncached. Our prefix cache and parallel encoding sped up only the first pass; more tokenizer processes add concurrency, not speed. The second pass was the tokenisation floor and grows with prompt length.

What we learned

  • For any model registered as vision-language, read the chat handler's text-to-ids path before tuning tokenisation. A hidden decode-and-re-encode caps what any first-pass cache can save.
  • When a profile shows the same work done twice, delete the duplicate before scaling it out. We added workers on Sep 27 and the second pass survived four more days.
  • Check that the code you optimise is on the critical path. Our cache cut the first encode to 0.013 s (<120k) while an uncached second encode still ran.
  • Prove an ids shortcut identical to the old round trip on recorded prompts (300/300 here) before spending GPU time; it was then adopted after a single run.

Caveats. Offline timings are single-process CPU. Online, the passthrough ran only on top of the shared cache (median 0.85 -> 0.54 s, one run each); it was never run alone. Requests with image, video or audio still take the text path and pay both passes. Their share of v3.1 traffic is not recorded in these sources. Production avoids the double pass: its Rust frontend (DYN_TOKENIZER=fastokens) tokenises and its workers skip tokenising (page_notes gap). The Sep 27 TPM jump also included a Triton kernel patch, so not all of 7.02 -> 12.34 M comes from the tokenizer workers.

What changed. Relaunched all four engines with production's attention numerics (training-compatible mode off) and an 8-bit KV cache instead of our 4-bit KV. Layout (tp2/dp2, DP attention, attention TP1), old arrival-pinned routing and load unchanged. (Oct 1 00:25 PDT (v3 run); idle A/B Sep 30 15:43; v2 Sep 30 16:23 (0.5x) and 20:43 (1.0x); GSM8K Oct 1 01:31; 3.34 M retest started Oct 1 21:29:59 PDT)

Exact change. chainN.sh: TRAINING_COMPAT=0 (sets SGLANG_M3_TRAINING_COMPATIBLE=0) and EXTRA_ENV="$BB SGLANG_MINIMAX_SPARSE_KV4=0" via launch_tp2x4_old.sh/launch.sh. Base: 4x tp2/ep2/dp2 DSpark, MAXREQ=64, MEMFRAC=0.68, CHUNK=32768, TOKW=4, HiCache ratio 3.0, SGLANG_TOKENIZE_PREFIX_CACHE=1. Replay: replay_v2.py v3 b00 frac 1.0 (no --skip-prod-shed). Idle A/B chain32.sh; v2 chain33.sh lever tc0kv8 and chain35.sh tc0kv8_1x; GSM8K gsm8k_bounded.py (chainD).

Why. Training-compat on routes spec verify through TrainingAttention's extend path and forces attention TP1; off, the production sparse backend runs and steps got cheaper (acceptance 3.37 vs 3.30 on v2). With DSpark and no MSA, our fork allows this only with 8-bit KV: twice the bytes per token, about half the cached tokens, so more re-prefill at 2.23 M.

What we learned

  • The production attention path lifted decode at every load tested: +22% idle, +29% at 1.36 M, +17% at 2.23 M, +37% at ~2.95 M (v2).
  • A KV-capacity cut hides until the working set overflows (hit 94.1 vs 94.3% at 1.36 M, 83.5 vs 94.4% at 2.23 M): test at target load.
  • GSM8K held (96.74% vs 96.21%) though greedy outputs diverge (3/30 identical); keep a GSM8K window on numerics runs.
  • If uniform, +17% would lift cap_lpm_075x's 3.34 M per-minute median decode (58.4) past 60 but not its worst minute (45.6); all 15 must pass.
  • At 3.34 M the cache loss wins: halving KV capacity turned a 17% decode gain at 2.23 M into a collapse at 3.34 M (Oct 1 22:29).

Caveats. Old test v3 with arrival-pinned routing: in the baseline one engine ran 49-56 requests while the others ran 2-13 (Sep 30 23:08); not the adopted stack. At 2.23 M the decode gain may be partly confounded by long queues (TTFT p90 168 s); idle (+22%) and 1.36 M at equal hit rate (+29%) are cleaner. Not yet measured at 3.34 M: v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8shid_tc0kv8_075x (tokenise-once stack, no decode-after-prefill, GSM8K window) started Oct 1 21:29:59 PDT. Under load at 1.36 M this path prefilled 32k+ uncached prompts slower (p50 5.0 vs 3.75 s), although idle single-stream TTFT was faster (1.43 vs 1.60 s). The 8-bit engine's pool size is not quoted in these sources; 'about half' comes from KV bytes per token (20:55 row). Errors 8 vs 6 of 3,234 on test v3 (before the literal-<image> fix); cause of the extra 2 not recorded.

What changed. No setting changed. Profiled one engine between levers (one cold 128k-token prompt, then 32-stream decode) and compared our layout and kernels with production's config. (Oct 1 05:05-05:25 PDT (profile); production config read Sep 27 23:15 and Sep 30 13:40 PDT)

Exact change. prof_prefill.sh <tag> [port]: POST /flush_cache, /start_profile; cold 131,072 random-token /v1/completions (max_tokens 1); then 32 x 2,048-token prompts x 256 tokens (ignore_eos); traces in /data01/minimax31/logs/prof-<tag>-{prefill,decode}; prof_top.py sums kernel time by name and class. Ran on v3_lp_075x engine e3 (port 19491) under serving/HOLD (prof_then_release.sh). Production: read-only serve.yaml + cmdline on b300-18.

Why. With speculative decoding plus DP attention, an engine's two GPUs step together, never mix prefill with decode, and run prefill first. Any prompt chunk on either GPU pauses decode on both, and our Triton prefill kernels run at ~12-14% of tensor-core peak, so more prompt work means more paused steps. Production runs attention TP2 without DP attention, with in-house kernels.

What we learned

  • Spec decoding plus DP attention pauses decode on both GPUs during any prefill step, so faster prefill kernels should lift decode, not only TTFT (expected, not measured).
  • Decode-after-prefill left 2.23 M decode unchanged (76.2 vs 77.6 tok/s): reordering keeps the same prefill work. Its 3.34 M run is queued, not measured.
  • Settings-only levers at 3.34 M (16k chunk, block 4, mem 0.76, cache-first) left decode at 46-57 tok/s; lockstep layout and prefill kernels are untested in the engine.
  • Profile between levers with the engine held (serving/HOLD): one cold 128k prefill plus a 32-stream decode trace ranks kernel targets by GPU seconds.

Caveats. One engine (e3, DP0), synthetic random-token prompts; the decode trace had low draft acceptance (05:05 row). Running requests per engine also grow with load (20-30 at 3.34 M, 37-56 at 4.42 M), which slows each step; the profile does not separate the two causes. The 2.23 M and 4.42 M points ran test v3 (incl. production-shed giant prompts); 3.34 M ran v3.1 (v3.1 at 2.23 M: 76.5 tok/s, v3_lp_05x_v31). Production's kernel speeds were not measured; the dashboard's '2-3x slower prompt processing' is an estimate (page_notes setup_compare). Production max running: 128 per worker in serve.yaml (Sep 30); the Sep 27 argv read showed 256. DP attention off is refused while training numerics are on (fork constraint; launch.sh refuses it unless FORCE_TOPOLOGY=1); not tested with training-compat off. decode-after-prefill and --enable-prefill-delayer at 3.34 M are queued, not measured (node_state.txt).

What changed. Repeated the best 2.23 M configuration on the same traffic as a noise check (r2, 19:10), after the v2 baseline repeat on Sep 30. The 19:10 row set the rule: a lever must move the pass count by 2+ minutes, or be repeated, before it is adopted or rejected. (Sep 30 07:05 PDT (v2 repeat); Oct 1 19:10 PDT (v3.1 repeat))

Exact change. v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8_05x_r2 repeats v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8_05x: /tr/v3/b00.jsonl frac 1.0 (2.23 M), protocol v3.1 (--skip-prod-shed), MEMFRAC=0.76, TOKW=8, XARGS='$HCX --schedule-policy lpm', ROUTE_PIN_BY_INFLIGHT=1, ROUTE_REPIN_SLACK=16 (chainQ.sh base_env). The r2 lever line is in node_state.txt; it started 18:27 PDT. v2 pair: chain28 v2e 0.5x and chain29 base2 (mem 0.68, --no-prime --img 1x1). Pairwise spreads were computed for this entry from runs_v3.json minutes[] (ttft_p50, ttft_p99, decode_p50) and are not in PROGRESS.md.

Why. Each minute is a pass/fail verdict on quantiles of one minute's traffic (179-274 requests). Between the identical runs, per-minute TTFT medians moved 0.061 s typically (max 0.216), p99 1.2 s (max 9.6) and decode 4.6 tok/s (max 10.0); 12-14 of 15 minutes sat within 0.2 s of the 1 s line, so misses wander.

What we learned

  • Treat a one-minute change in pass count as noise; require a 2+ minute move or a repeat before adopting or rejecting a lever.
  • Rank levers on continuous per-minute margins (median TTFT, decode) alongside pass counts; counts flip when minutes sit within 0.1-0.2 s of a threshold.
  • Buy margin, not a bare pass: 1.79 M misses were 0.02-0.19 s over 1 s, so the floor had to drop 0.2-0.3 s for a robust pass.
  • At 3.34 M, 10 of the best run's 15 minutes decode within 4.6 tok/s of 60, the typical repeat move: its 4/15 is fragile, so repeat 3.34 M winners.
  • Twin runs (both groups replay the same half of the sessions) resolve ~1.5 tok/s in one run; per-minute pass counts per group stay noisy (10/15 vs 10/15 here, but single minutes differ by up to 13 tok/s).

Caveats. Only two identical real-traffic pairs exist (v2 at 1.36 M, v3.1 at 2.23 M). Noise at 3.34 M is not measured, and the 4.6 tok/s decode spread comes from 2.23 M. Spreads come from the 15 paired minutes of one pair; the maxima are single minutes. The pass-count noise shown is under the old rule; under the Oct 1 SLA both repeats pass 15/15. The three 1.79 M runs differ in config, so their shifting misses mix noise with small lever effects. Between the two runs, env-gated patches (parallel tokenise 16:15, warm bypass 17:45) were added to the engine tree and left off.

What changed. Benchmarked MiniMax's open-source (MIT) MSA prompt-attention kernel against our Triton kernel on identical inputs in our packed KV layout, wrote an engine adapter, and tried to run both inside our engine image. (Oct 1 06:25-09:45 PDT)

Exact change. kernels/bench_msa_vs_triton.py (MSA sparse_atten_nvfp4_kv_func vs fork q8kv4_sparse_attention; FP8 Q, random packed NVFP4 K/V + E4M3 scales, top-16 blocks, pattern local, T=16384) in lmsysorg/sglang:dev-cu13-minimax-m3 (fmha_sm100 0.1.1 @fdc49e7, CuTe-DSL 4.5.2) on GPU 7 (window_msa_devimage.sh); adapter kernels/msa_nvfp4_adapter.py (SGLANG_Q8KV4_MSA_SPARSE=1, SGLANG_MSA_CUTE_DIR) + test_msa_adapter.py; image tests window_msa_ourimage.sh (A/B/T1/T2), window_msa_t3.sh (T3/T4); our image minimax-m31-sglang:demo-bef87f4.

Why. Sparse attention (partial + combine) is ~30% of prefill GPU time (05:25 profile), so a ~2x kernel should shorten each prompt chunk and, via the two-GPU lockstep, each decode pause (not measured). MSA takes contiguous K/V, so the adapter gathers paged K/V and swizzles scales: ~1.5 ms extra on a 2.16 ms kernel call (09:45).

What we learned

  • Standalone kernel speedups shrink in the engine's call shape: 1.93-2.47x alone became 1.24-1.29x on a mixed engine-like batch once K/V gather and scale swizzle were included.
  • Check a kernel's DSL toolchain before porting: CuTe-DSL 4.5.2 (MSA) and 4.6.2 (our image) cannot share one Python process.
  • Bit-exact output on our packed KV layout means a swap can be validated by a parity test (the fork's MSA gate asserts bit-identity) rather than a quality run.
  • The remaining kernel-side step is fusing the K/V gather (estimated ~1.85x), once the toolchain clash is solved.

Caveats. No engine run with MSA: end-to-end prefill, TTFT and decode gains are not measured. Synthetic inputs: random KV bytes and a 'local' top-16 block pattern; the adapter test is one mixed batch. The adapter is eager-only (never used under CUDA-graph capture). The adapter targets the Triton sparse attention of our current training-numerics prefill path; it does not unlock training-compat off with 4-bit KV, whose guard also forbids spec decoding.

What changed. No engine change: we split each slow request into time segments and read the per-rank engine log around it. (Sep 28 16:35 PDT (first anatomy, older v1 staircase); Oct 1 04:35 PDT (test v3); Oct 1 20:05 PDT (engine-log anatomy on tok8sh_05x).)

Exact change. slow_reqs.py (to_sched / queue / prefill / first content per request from ReqTimeStats; needs --enable-request-time-stats-logging); reqstats_join.py; log-only patch_timestats_detail.py; engine logs kept at teardown by launch_tp2x4_old.sh (logs/engine-<ts>-tp2-<i>.log); tail_anatomy.py (Sep 28); replay_v2.py --skip-prod-shed defines test v3.1.

Why. The scheduler admits the in-progress chunked request first with the whole step budget (16k tokens per rank), so a giant takes every step on its rank until done. Prefill precedes decode and spec + DP attention never mix them, so both ranks stop decoding; new arrivals on that rank, even a 1k-token or 9k warm prompt, queue behind it.

What we learned

  • Most tail victims are bystanders: 31 of 43 requests over 15 s needed <8k uncached tokens (Oct 1); 33 of the 60 slowest (>12 s) needed <4k (Sep 28).
  • Read the per-rank engine log: back-to-back 'Prefill batch' lines with #new-seq 1 and a rising #queue-req mark a monopolising chunk.
  • Split slow requests by segment (to scheduler, queue, prefill, first visible content): the three tail kinds need different fixes.
  • Replay only what production served: 3 of 5 spike clusters were giant prompts production had refused with HTTP 429.

Caveats. The engine-log trace is one rank in one ~19-s window; the 47-request split is one run (tok8sh_05x). p99 left the SLA on Oct 1, but the same freeze stops decode, which is still a rule. The v3 → v3.1 p99 change also includes the media-tag fix (6 HTTP 500s → 0). Production caps outstanding uncached prefill at 600k tokens per worker (admission); we have none. page_notes rates that difference 'Small'.

What changed. Raised the gateway container's open-file limit so it can hold many more client and engine connections at once. (Found Oct 1 03:20 PDT from v3_lp_1x (ended 03:15 PDT); raised before v3_lp_05x (ended 03:56 PDT).)

Exact change. run_gateway.sh and regw.sh: docker run --ulimit nofile=65536:524288 for container m31-gateway (alphabeta-m31 commit a042954, Oct 1 03:29 PDT; its message includes 'gateway nofile fix'). Context: since patch_shim_poolrank.py (Sep 30 21:30 PDT), shim.py line 123 opens upstream clients with httpx.Limits(max_connections=None, max_keepalive_connections=None). Before that, httpx's default capped each engine at 100 connections.

Why. The gateway ran with a soft open-file limit of 1,024 (engines 65,535). Each streamed request holds a client and an upstream socket; since Sep 30 21:30 PDT the upstream pool is uncapped (httpx default: 100 per engine). At 4.42 M, with TTFT p99 132.5 s holding streams open, descriptors most likely ran out and new connections failed at 0.0 s.

What we learned

  • Set nofile explicitly on every proxy container: the gateway ran at a soft limit of 1,024 while the engines had 65,535, and it failed only at peak load.
  • Under a 100%-success SLA one error fails a minute: at 4.42 M, 33 errors (27 ReadErrors, 6 media-tag 500s) touched 10 of 15 minutes.
  • Removing a connection-pool cap moves the limit to the process file-descriptor limit; raise both together and test at peak in-flight, not average.
  • Audit every proxy limit before a load test: gateway caps already turned Sep 27 replays into 105 and 8,094 HTTP 429s (caps: in-flight 64 + TPM 10 M; in-flight 512).

Caveats. Not re-validated at 4.42 M. Later runs (≤3.34 M, test v3.1) also carry the media-tag fix and skip production-429 requests, so their 0 errors do not prove the fix alone. The link is inferred. No descriptor counts were logged; PROGRESS 03:20 lists the ReadErrors and the 1,024 limit side by side, and page_notes attributes the resets to the limit. The uncapped upstream pool's role is also inferred. Two earlier bursts may share the cause but were never root-caused: Sep 28 02:05 PDT chain13 (53 ReadErrors at 6x, before the pool was uncapped) and Sep 30 23:18 PDT GSM8K (1,008 gateway→engine 502s and 304 client ConnectErrors, all 1,319 requests sent at once).

NUMA binding of half the engines caused OOM kills of the other half RejectedGroup B's automatic NUMA binding restricted its host-cache memory to nodes 0-1; the kernel OOM killer then stopped group-A engines during boot.
MeasureBeforeAfterSource
engines healthy after 25 min boot4/4 (unbound)2/4 (B bound, OOM kills at 02:08, 02:14, 02:21 UTC)launch TIMEOUT; dmesg

What changed. Twin v3_ab_numa_cl_1x: group B containers with --cap-add SYS_NICE so the engine binds scheduler CPUs and memory to a NUMA node. (Oct 3 19:00-19:45 PDT)

Exact change. launch.sh NUMA_CAP=1; fork utils/numa_utils.py binding.

Why. Node 0008 has 4 NUMA nodes of about 755 GB; GPU pair n sits on node n. One engine needs about 580 GB of host memory (2 ranks x 273 GB of cache pools). The binding gave engine 3 a policy for nodes 0-1, where engines 0-1 already hold their pools, so the bound allocation could not fit.

What we learned

  • Pin all engines or none: a pinned engine can push an unpinned engine out of memory.
  • Check the bound node against the topology (nvidia-smi topo -m) before a run; use explicit per-engine CPUSET/MEMS pins.

Caveats. The exact mapping fault (logical vs physical GPU index) is inferred, not traced.

What changed. Tried production's attention numerics while keeping our 4-bit KV cache, on the tokenise-once stack at 3.34 M. (Oct 1 21:25-21:30 PDT (first seen Sep 27 13:38 PDT))

Exact change. chainQ lever v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8shid_tc0_075x (started 04:24:58 UTC): TRAINING_COMPAT=0 with launch.sh defaults SGLANG_MINIMAX_SPARSE_KV4=1 and SGLANG_DISABLE_MSA=1; SPEC=dspark, MEMFRAC=0.76, TOKW=8, --schedule-policy lpm, --enable-request-time-stats-logging. Aborted by killing chainQ, watchdog and the waiting launcher by PID; chainQ restarted; next lever v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8shid_tc0kv8_075x (TRAINING_COMPAT=0 + 8-bit KV) started 04:29:59 UTC.

Why. With training-compat off, attention uses the production sparse backend. In our 0922 fork its 4-bit-KV mode requires blk128 MSA, FP8 queries, a max-score indexer and no speculative decoding. Our image has no usable MSA (launch.sh sets SGLANG_DISABLE_MSA=1) and every config runs DSpark, so the guard fires at init. Production runs this path with in-house KV4 kernels (kv4_fused_verify_attn etc.).

What we learned

  • Read a backend's init guards before queuing a numerics lever: this refusal was logged Sep 27 13:38 PDT and in chain32.sh (Sep 30), yet cost another boot window.
  • Production numerics with 4-bit KV need a KV4 attention kernel the guard accepts (MSA or our own) and KV4 verify that works with speculative decoding.
  • Until then, production numerics come only with 8-bit KV, at about half the cache capacity.

Caveats. Whether the guard reflects a hard kernel limit or a conservative check was not tested. Production's KV4 kernels are not available to us (owner rule: learn settings, do not copy their image or kernels). Lever lines are truncated in the node snapshot (node_state.txt); only the listed knobs are confirmed.

What changed. Ran Dynamo 1.5.0's KV-cache-aware router (the base of production's router, stock build) instead of our gateway's routing, in front of four workers with the same engine settings. First with production-like settings, then with stronger cache affinity. Our gateway stayed in front only to translate the API (no session pinning). (Oct 1 01:25 PDT (dyn_05x) and 02:15 PDT (dyn2_05x); routing kept in our gateway at 02:21 PDT.)

Exact change. chainD.sh: dynamo/frontend.sh (dynamo.frontend --router-mode kv --router-replica-sync --router-temperature 0 --dyn-chat-processor sglang --dyn-preprocess-workers 8 --migration-limit 3) + FRONTEND_EXTRA='--router-prefill-load-scale 1.0 --router-kv-overlap-score-credit 1.0 --router-kv-overlap-score-credit-decay 0.5 --active-prefill-tokens-threshold 600000'. Workers via dynamo/up.sh WORKER_TP=2: tp2/ep2/dp2, MAXREQ 64, CHUNK 32768, image demo-dynamo, tree 0922-sglang-hicache, MEMFRAC=0.68, DSpark bidir window 4095, HiCache ratio 3. Gateway: ROUTE_SESSION_KEY= ROUTE_DP_SIZE=0. chainD2.sh restarted only the frontend: overlap credit 3.0, decay 0.0, no busy threshold.

Why. Each of our engines runs DP attention: two ranks, two prefix caches. In our runs Dynamo chose the engine but did not pin the DP rank, so a returning session could land on the sibling rank and re-prefill its conversation; any prefill pauses decode on both ranks. Production runs DP attention off: one cache per worker, matching Dynamo's routing unit.

What we learned

  • A cache-aware router works only if its routing unit equals the cache unit; with DP attention each rank holds its own cache, so the router must pick the rank.
  • Affinity tuning did not fix the granularity mismatch: tripling the overlap credit and removing its decay and busy threshold lifted hit only from 65.2% to 70.8%.
  • Borrow a production component together with the topology it assumes: production's router faces one cache per worker (DP attention off); ours faced two.
  • Judge any router change first by cache hit and cold-prefill count: hit fell 24-29 points and 32k+ cold prefills rose 7-9x, matching the latency collapse.

Caveats. Stock Dynamo 1.5.0 only approximated production. The fleet's strict-affinity policy (min 2 blocks, >50% overlap) and admission-control flags are not in 1.5.0 (frontend.sh), and session-pin Redis was not used. Dynamo's frontend did its own templating and tokenisation (--dyn-chat-processor sglang; production uses dynamo), so our engines' tokenisation prefix cache was not in the path. One run per setting, at 2.23 M on test v3; the planned 1.0x Dynamo run was skipped. Re-test only once our engines can run DP attention off (production's layout). Our build requires DP attention because TRAINING_COMPAT=1 forces attention TP1. Baseline is arrival pinning (hit 94.4%); load-aware pinning later reached 94.6% on the same test.

What changed. Four single-factor changes, each on the then-adopted stack: give waiting requests half of each prefill step, halve the prefill chunk, let warm requests jump uncached chunks, double requests per engine. (Test v3.1, Oct 1 PDT rows: CHUNK=16384 08:50, 128/engine 12:05, fair share 13:05, warm bypass 18:30; test v2 checks Sep 29 22:10 – Sep 30 18:39; fair-share crashes Sep 28 21:16 and Oct 1 06:17 PDT.)

Exact change. SGLANG_CHUNKED_REQ_SHARE=0.5 (patch_fair_chunk.py + patch_fair_chunk_v2.py + patch_chunk_oom_guard.py); CHUNK=16384 (--chunked-prefill-size, default 32768; SGLang splits it across the 2 DP ranks, so 16k → 8k per rank); SGLANG_WARM_BYPASS_TOKENS=8192 SGLANG_WARM_BYPASS_MAX_SKIPS=1 (patch_warm_bypass.py); MAXREQ=128 (--max-running-requests; lever line MEMFRAC=0.76 MAXREQ=128). All reverted: share 1.0, CHUNK 32768, bypass env unset, MAXREQ 64.

Why. Likely: under the DP lockstep, smaller prefill pieces (CHUNK=16384; half-step fair share) add prefill steps without cutting prefill work, and each prefill step pauses decode on both GPUs. Warm requests rarely queued (p50 0.007 s), so the bypass could not move the median; with one skip it left 2 minutes over 15 s. Engines ran 20–30 of 64 allowed requests.

What we learned

  • Under rank lockstep, slicing prefill finer cost decode at load (fair share helped slightly or tied at 1.36 M, lost at 3.34 M); interleaving decode steps fixed the tail instead.
  • Measure the wait before building a bypass: warm requests queued 0.007 s median (17:05, before the 17:45 patch), and parking chunks gained nothing.
  • Check that a cap binds before raising it: engines ran 20–30 requests against a limit of 64 at 3.34 M (v3_lp_075x).
  • Carry known boot fixes into new lever lines: 128/engine booted Sep 28 only with a 1 GiB flashinfer workspace (mem 0.66); Oct 1 set neither (failure undiagnosed).
  • Production's host-overhead flags (plan stream, incremental streaming, local control broadcast, recv interval 2) cost 2.15 tok/s on our stack (twin run Oct 2 03:14, CI −3.7..−0.5): settings tuned for production's layout do not transfer automatically.

Caveats. Single runs; identical runs differ by about one minute (PROGRESS 19:10 PDT 10-01). Warm bypass was tested only at 2.23 M, where every v3.1 config passes the current SLA. Production's warm_bypass is an admission outcome counter (warm_cache_hit_ratio 0.9, max_outstanding_uncached_prefill_tokens 600000), which we did not test. Warm queueing is rare, not absent: the 20:05 tail anatomy (tok8sh_05x) found small or warm requests queued 10–21 s behind giants. The Oct 1 128/engine boot failure was not diagnosed; differences from the Sep 28 runs that booted (chain17.sh b128ws, chain19.sh t8r64) include mem 0.76 vs 0.66, no 1 GiB SGLANG_FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_SIZE, and the HiCache tree with HiCache on. Fair share 0.875 when requests wait (dap_s875) was dropped untested.

What changed. We tried three things: more tokenizer processes per engine (8 instead of 4), a single process with a large cache, and splitting long prompts into pieces tokenised on parallel threads. TOKW=8 stayed in the stack (verdict: no clear change). The single process and both parallel variants were rejected and are off. (Oct 1 15:00-19:10 PDT (earlier TOKW tests: Sep 28 and Sep 30))

Exact change. TOKW=8 / TOKW=1 (launch_tp2x4_old.sh passes --tokenizer-worker-num ${TOKW}); TOKW=1 ran with SGLANG_TOKENIZE_PREFIX_CACHE_ENTRIES=4096 (default 512). Parallel: patch_tok_parallel.py on tok_prefix_cache.py (hicache tree, backup .pre-tokpar). On a miss or a long tail (>= SGLANG_TOKENIZE_PARALLEL_MIN_CHARS=40000) it splits at special-token boundaries, runs Rust encode_batch and sets TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=true. Tested with SGLANG_TOKENIZE_PARALLEL_CHUNKS=16 + RAYON_NUM_THREADS=16, then 4 chunks with the default pool. Now unset. Tags: v3_lp_cap_lpm_tok8_05x, _tok8_05x_r2, _tok8_0375x, _tok1_05x, _tok8par_05x, _tok8par4_05x.

Why. The cache and parallel encode sped up only the first encode; more processes add concurrency, not speed. The uncached second encode still ran on every request, so the median barely moved. A single process also carries all HTTP and SSE streaming and became the bottleneck. Parallel threads most likely took CPU from the GPU schedulers; decode and p99 worsened.

What we learned

  • Require a move of 2+ minutes or a repeat run. Identical TOKW=8 runs scored 10/15 and 11/15, so 9 vs 10 is noise.
  • A bit-exact parallel encode that cut a full encode's offline median from 0.281 to 0.073 s still regressed online. Extra CPU threads can starve the GPU schedulers; watch decode too.
  • Don't funnel traffic into one process just to get cache hits: the tokenizer process also serves HTTP and streaming. Share the cache instead.
  • Process count sets throughput, not the latency floor: 2->8 per engine lifted the static frame 5.65->7.82 M/GPU; 4->8 moved the 2.23 M median only 0.94->0.90-0.92 s.

Caveats. Parallel encoding was tested while the second encode still ran on every request. It was not retested on the tokenise-once stack. That the parallel threads starved the schedulers is inferred from p99 and decode. No CPU profile of these runs is recorded. tok8par_05x was aborted after 8 minutes; runs_v3 keeps 9 partial-minute bins (1,461 requests), so its 0.95 M/GPU TPM is not comparable with full runs. TOKW=8 on test v2 (Sep 30 12:26 PDT) also left the median unchanged (0.90 s) and cut p99 by 25%. Re-scored on the current SLA, TOKW=1 and 4-chunk parallel also pass 15/15 (STANDINGS); the rejections rest on the old 1 s / 15 s rule, plus decode for 16 chunks.

What changed. Shortened the DSpark draft block from 7 to 4 tokens (production's draft uses 4) at 3.34 M, everything else equal. (Oct 1 07:58 PDT; acceptance history Sep 27 19:10 to Oct 1 21:25 PDT)

Exact change. chainQ lever v3_lp_cap_blk4_075x: MEMFRAC=0.76 DSPARK_BLOCK=4 (launch.sh adds --speculative-dspark-block-size 4); baseline v3_lp_cap_075x leaves DSPARK_BLOCK empty (our DSpark port defaults to 7: resolve_gamma(default=7)). Both: SPEC=dspark, DRAFT_ATTN=flashinfer, DRAFT_WINDOW=4095, SGLANG_DSPARK_M31_BIDIR_DRAFT=1, SGLANG_Q8KV4_SORT_MIN_LANES=1e12. Acceptance from accept_metrics.sh: delta(generated tokens - requests) / delta(spec_verify_calls).

Why. Each verify step runs the target model once. Block 4 accepted fewer tokens per step (3.06 vs 3.66), so the same replay needed 27% more verify steps (1,247,501 vs 981,478) and decode fell 15% (54.7→46.3 tok/s), in line with the 16% acceptance drop. Our DSpark port defaults to block 7; production's block 4 pairs with its DFlash2 draft.

What we learned

  • Tune block size per draft and traffic: production's block 4 pairs with DFlash2; our DSpark accepts 3.06 at block 4 vs 3.66 at 7 (M3: block 8 beat 4).
  • Our higher acceptance (3.66 vs production's reported 2.75-3.04) did not make decode faster than production's (54.7 vs 64.8 tok/s); production's config notes DSpark wins only at low concurrency.
  • Judge drafts on real-traffic metric deltas: a 3-prompt probe showed 5.79 accepted tokens per step, real replays 3.60-3.76.
  • Spec decoding pays only with CUDA graphs: c6 per stream 135 tok/s with graphs vs 19 for the vendor's eager DSpark and 37 without spec (Sep 27 19:10 PDT).

Caveats. One run per block size at 3.34 M; identical runs differ by about one minute (Oct 1 19:10). The Sep 28 v1 test agreed (block 4 staircase accept 3.33 vs 4.07). We have not run production's DFlash2 draft; DFlash2 vs DSpark not compared on our engine. Production's fa4 draft attention tested only on v2 at 1.36 M (Sep 30 11:44): 9/15, accept 3.30 vs 3.40, no gain. Production's decode (64.8) and acceptance (2.75-3.04) come from its own fleet load, not from our 3.34 M replay.

What changed. AB_B_SIDE=0 in the A words puts the B change on engines 0-1. (Oct 4 06:36-09:08 PDT)

Exact change. chainQ.sh and launch_tp2x4_old.sh support it; AB_B_SIDE stays exported in the chain shell, so set it on every twin line.

Why. Some host-side asymmetry (not GPU clocks or power caps: equal SW power-cap time, no HW slowdown) makes engines 2-3 slower at high decode rates.

What we learned

  • Run close calls twice with swapped sides and average.
  • Adoptions measured with B on engines 2-3 were conservative.

Caveats. The bias was absent in the 10-02 A/A at 0.75x; it may depend on load or host conditions.

What changed. From Oct 1 04:30, every replay leaves out the requests production itself refused with HTTP 429, and the literal '<image>' text bug that produced HTTP 500s is fixed. Production's logged results for exactly the replayed requests are scored minute by minute with the same rule and shown next to ours. (Oct 1, 04:30 PDT (v3.1); 10:00 PDT (production scored per minute))

Exact change. replay_v2.py --skip-prod-shed drops every trace record with prod_status == 429, in the warm-up and measured windows; their logged retries stay. chainQ.sh lever() runs replay_v2.py --traces /tr/v3/b00.jsonl[,/tr/v3/b01.jsonl] --last-frac <f> --measure-from 15000 --measure-to 15900 --warm-window 3600 --warm-inflight 32 --no-prime --img 1x1 --skip-prod-shed, with --flush-urls set to the 4 engines. patch_mm_literal_tags.py is applied to both engine trees. extract_runs.py writes runs_v3.json with per-minute TTFT p50/p99, decode p50 (streams with >= 20 tokens) and errors, for ours and for production (prod_ttft = hub upstream header_time, prod_total = response_time, prod_status; traffic_extract_v2.py). Our errors count only on requests production answered 200. Loads: b00 frac 0.75 = 1.79 M, b00 = 2.23 M, b00 + half of b01 = 3.34 M, b00 + b01 = 4.42 M.

Why. Production's admission caps cold work at 600k uncached tokens per worker and refuses the excess with HTTP 429. Replaying those requests gave our engine work production never did: 3 of the 4 at 2.23 M were 357-420k-token cold prompts, each holding a DP rank 20-35 s in 16k chunks while its other requests waited.

What we learned

  • Replay only work the reference served: 3 production-refused cold giants (357-420k tokens) seeded 3 of 5 stall clusters at 2.23 M; dropping them left TTFT-failing minutes at 6.
  • Read prod_status before production's token counts: a 429 logs prompt and cached tokens as 0, which looks like zero uncached work.
  • Score production per minute on the same requests with the same rule: on valid runs it passed every latency and decode minute, so misses beyond its own errors are ours.
  • Budget the replay tail: measured phases ran 1,456-1,535 s for a 900 s window at 3.34 M, about 10 idle-GPU minutes per lever.

Caveats. The 7 → 9/15 equals the 2 error-only minutes (m4, m6) fixed by the literal-<image> patch bundled into v3.1. TTFT-failing minutes stayed at 6: p99 recovered in m2, m9 and m10 but failed anew in m12 and m13. Run p99 differed 9.80 vs 12.85 s between identical runs, so the 18.28 → 14.28 s drop is near noise; the case for v3.1 rests on the traced stall clusters. TTFT definitions differ. Ours is the first content, reasoning or tool delta at the client. Production's is the hub upstream header_time, which matched its frontend first-token histogram (Sep 30 13:40). Fidelity gaps remain: images are sent as 1x1 (on v2, image-request prompts were 0.872x production's, Sep 29 16:15) and there is no priming. Cache hit also trails production (95.4% vs 96.8%, tok8shid_05x). At 4.42 M, 84% of the extra uncached tokens came from evicted sessions and 15% from sessions first seen in the replay (Oct 1 03:45). The load axis is production's request logs; its engines counted 1.1x the requests and 1.45x the prompt tokens per request (Sep 30 13:40). Production passing every minute holds for valid runs only. In the partial record of v3_lp_f2_075x (engine crash 06:17, stopped 06:21), production's decode fell below 60 in 2 minutes (53.1, 50.9). TPM credits the window with tokens that finished in the tail; counting only tokens served inside the window is planned, not built.

What changed. Built three first-token instruments on real traffic. First, 30-second snapshots of the engines' latency histograms, reduced to per-minute deltas. Second, wall-clock stamps at each hand-off inside the engine, joined per request to the replay's send time. Third, a join of the client's first-token time against the gateway's own record, to price packet merging. (Oct 1, 19:00-20:45 PDT)

Exact change. metrics_sampler.sh: curl /metrics on ports 19191/19291/19391/19491 every 30 s, filtered to 10 sglang metric families, → /data01/minimax31/logs/metrics. metrics_breakdown.py: per-minute histogram bucket deltas; rest = engine TTFT − queue − prefill_forward − request_process (means). patch_timestats_detail.py: log-only, needs --enable-request-time-stats-logging; logs TokTimeStats created/tokenized/dispatch/dispatched/first_token at WARNING, and ReqTimeStats gains recv/fwd/prefill_done. replay_v2.py records resp_id/sent_wall/first_chunk, and reqstats_join.py joins them to the engine stamps. analyze_lever.sh <tag> [live] runs both. coalesce_gap.py joins replay TTFT to the gateway access-log ttft on prompt/completion/cached tokens. launch_tp2x4_old.sh saves outgoing engine logs (logs/engine-<ts>-tp2-<i>.log). patch_shim_firstnow.py adds STREAM_COALESCE_FIRST_NOW=1 (built, default off).

Why. Engine TTFT runs from the HTTP handler to the first token at the tokenizer process. Histograms showed queue p50 0.00 s and prefill p50 0.21-0.24 s; subtracting means left 0.65-1.02 s outside the scheduler in both the measured window and the low-load tail. Per-request wall-clock stamps split it into gateway, tokenise, IPC and return segments.

What we learned

  • Before optimising tokenisation, trace the text→ids path: four tokenisation levers failed to lower the median because the VLM path decoded the prompt and re-encoded it downstream of the cache.
  • Use the replay's low-load tail as a free control: the outside-scheduler time stayed 0.69-1.02 s at 7-67 req/min, so it was a load-independent per-request cost.
  • Measure small effects by joining logs, not by A/B pass counts: the gateway-to-client gap is 0.018 s median; two v2 coalescing A/Bs read neutral inside ±1-minute noise.
  • Point the same instruments at decode: metrics_sampler.sh already records inter_token_latency_seconds and forward_execution_seconds_total, but metrics_breakdown.py does not parse them yet.

Caveats. The second encode was found by reading serving_chat (19:20), not by the timers. mm_ids_verify.py sized it offline (p50 0.131 s, p90 0.695 s), and tok8shid confirmed it on GPU (20:45). py-spy had already shown each prompt tokenised twice on Sep 27 (13:09 PDT; PROGRESS row 20:09 UTC). It was read as a throughput cap and answered with 8 tokenizer workers. Engine-metric TTFT means already put the time before the scheduler on Sep 28 (ttft_breakdown.sh, 12:25). New on Oct 1 were per-minute deltas on real traffic, per-request stamps and the gateway join. Tokenizer worker processes drop INFO logs, so the stamps moved to WARNING; one run's time stats were lost at teardown before the launcher saved engine logs (13:05). Histogram quantiles are interpolated from coarse buckets; the outside-scheduler remainder uses means. The decode-after-prefill tail gain (p99 10.80 → 8.22 s) comes from one run; identical runs differed 9.80 vs 12.85 s in run p99. Warm 200k+ prompts still tokenise slowly in the tail (p75 3.27 s, p90 4.25 s; 336 requests), even though offline replay hits the cache almost every time. Cause not established; CPU contention in the engine cpuset is the next suspect. The gateway join matched 3,013 of 3,043 streaming requests on token counts and measures coalescing plus delivery (an upper bound). The first-packet flush (STREAM_COALESCE_FIRST_NOW=1) is built but has not been run.
